entry.title: SAP BTP - IS - Beyond the Tool: Frankenstein Landscapes, Art. Sprawl and Integration Storytelling
entry.content:
Knowledge becomes easier to retain when the problem becomes a story.

Teach the problem first. The tool comes later.

Before teaching the tool, make the problem visible.

 

In less than six months, without dedicated budget or corporate support, I produced more than 10 technical articles here in the SAP Community, 30+ articles on other platforms, seven DOI-published specifications representing two architectures DEIP and SDIA, an open-source Kafka adapter, SAP CITS, and the SDIA Control Plane, currently under development.

But producing more was not enough.

I realized that I also needed to improve how I communicate architectural thinking, making complex problems easier for professionals at different levels to understand.

That led me to spend the last three months studying storytelling, visual learning, and scenario-based approaches. The research I reviewed reinforced the direction: narrative formats can improve comprehension and recall.

So this is the new approach I am bringing to the SAP Community: technical problems, development challenges, design decisions, and architecture presented through visual film storytelling first — with the technical depth behind it.

My objective is simple: make knowledge easier to enter, understand, and retain.

Visual Cognition → Abstraction → Perception → Action → Knowledge Sharing → Acknowledgement

The goal is not to reduce technical depth. It is to activate understanding earlier, before the reader reaches the implementation layer.

A Different Way to Learn Integration Architecture

My approach will continue to include written explanations, architecture diagrams, and technical depth. But when the subject allows it, I will also use short narrative films to introduce the problem through an incident, a decision, or a realistic architectural situation.

The objective is simple: create an easier entry point before moving into product-specific terminology and implementation.

The difference is the entry point: story first, implementation later.

Tools change. Architectural problems usually do not.

Frankenstein Landscape - DEIP solves.

A Frankenstein Landscape is not defined by the number of technologies, but by the absence of a coherent architecture above them. 

When platforms, capabilities, ownership, and responsibilities evolve independently, fragmentation follows: teams become tool-centric, governance weakens, and knowledge becomes isolated.

The problem is rarely another tool.
It is the absence of architecture above the tools.

Story Telling Class - Architecture Film of Frankenstein Landscape:

The short film above presents this problem through a storytelling format rather than through a traditional architecture presentation.

From Platform Fragmentation to Artifact Sprawl

Artifact Sprawl happens when integration artifacts grow without clear structure, ownership, traceability, or lifecycle control.

Even technically correct flows, APIs, Packages, Iflows, mappings, credentials, certificates, queues, and runtime resources can become difficult to govern, trace and undeploy retire at scale.

Platform fragmentation can amplify the problem, but even a single platform can suffer from severe sprawl.

The solution is structure, ownership, and governance above the tool.

Artifact Sprawl - SDIA solves.

The next short film looks at the same landscape from another perspective: the organization and governance of the integration artifacts themselves.

Video — Artifact Sprawl

The central question is no longer only which platform contains the integration?

It becomes:

Which domain owns it?

Which capability does it support?

Which other artifacts and runtime resources depend on it?

Who understands it?

And when the integration is no longer required, can we confidently retire everything associated with it?

Those questions become increasingly important as integration landscapes grow.

 Closing

I have tried to bring this content to the highest level of clarity, visual quality, and technical depth I can currently produce.

I have not personally come across many technical articles in the SAP Community using this type of storytelling approach, so I decided to experiment with it.

If this format helps you understand or remember the subject more easily, then it has achieved its purpose. If not, that is perfectly fine as well — people learn in different ways.

There is already content covering HTTPS, SOAP, API Management, TCP/IP, and the OSI model, and the next topic planned for release this week is AMQP, MQTT, and Quality of Service (QoS).

If there is a specific integration or architecture topic you would like to see presented in this format, leave it in the comments. It may become one of the next stories.

And one small disclaimer: please do not ask me for a tutorial on how these films are produced. That part took a considerable amount of time to learn. At the moment, I am the writer, script editor, director, editor, technical reviewer, and everything else in between.

So, no classes on that part. 🙂

Thank you for reading  and for watching.

Ricardo Viana.

entry.title: SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Handling Missing Public APIs as a Partner — A Practical Guide
entry.content:
SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Handling Missing Public APIs as a Partner — A Practical Guide

Introduction

During SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition implementations and partner custom developments, partners occasionally encounter a scenario where a required API simply does not exist in the SAP Business Accelerator Hub. This gap can become a project blocker — particularly when third-party integrations or BTP side-by-side extensions depend on data objects that have no released API endpoint. During developer extensibiltiy on-stack customization of  SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition some of the required entities are not released for partner developement.

This blog post consolidates the recommended guidance for SAP partners on how to handle such situations. It covers the permanent resolution path via the SAP Customer Influence Programme (CIP), interim workaround options using Custom APIs, current known limitations, and the product improvements on SAP's roadmap.

Whether you are an implementation consultant, solution architect, partner enablement lead, or a partner developer, this guide provides the end-to-end picture.

The Scenario

You are mid-implementation of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition or in the process of building partner add-on of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Your solution requires an API — either to expose data to a BTP extension or to support an on-stack integration — and it is nowhere to be found on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub.

Before raising alarms, it is important to understand the two distinct types of APIs involved:

  • Local APIs — CDS views, Business Object Interfaces used in On-Stack Extensionsibility using ABAP Cloud
  • Remote APIs — APIs consumed externally, typically by BTP side-by-side applications or third-party systems.

This distinction determines both the CIP campaign you should target and the workaround approach you should implement in the interim.

Permanent Solution: The SAP Customer Influence Programme (CIP)

The right long-term path for any missing API on SAP Business Accelerator Hub is a formal request through the SAP Customer Influence Programme. Here is the recommended step-by-step process:

Note: SAP Continuos Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (CIP) would be moved to new Aha platform in near future and after the migration the CIP sessions and request URLs will be redirected to the Aha! platform after go-live.

Step 1 — Verify the API is Genuinely Missing

Before submitting any request, search SAP Business Accelerator Hub thoroughly. Confirm the API does not exist in any form — sometimes a different naming convention or an OData version difference can cause confusion.

Note: Please try out Joule copilot in SAP Business Accelerator Hub , It helps you with all your queries on the content available.

Note: make sure to select SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition in the product list in the SAP Business Accelerator Hub

Step 2 — Determine the API Type

Classify the missing API as either a Local API (on-stack) or a Remote API (external/BTP-facing). This classification determines which CIP campaign to use.

Step 3 — Check for an Existing CIP Request

Search the relevant campaign before creating a new entry. If another partner has already submitted the same request:

  • Vote for it. Every vote increases priority visibility with the SAP product team.

If no matching request exists, submit a new one. for more details please refer to SAP Community - Continuous Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition

Step 4 — Submit via the Correct CIP Campaign

 

API TypeCIP Campaign LinkNotes
Remote APIsCampaign 1175For APIs consumed by external apps or BTP side-by-side extensions (Loosely Couple Extensions using SAP BTP)
Local APIsCampaign 2759For on-stack APIs consumed within the SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public system (Tightly Couple Extension using ABAP Cloud)

SLA Note: SAP targets a response within 20 business days of submission. For priority cases, partners can escalate via a partner support ticket / partner escallation channel.

For more detaila about CIP please refer to details below:

  • SAP Continuous Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition - Frequently Asked Questions
  • SAP Continuous Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Public Edition - Session List and Rules of Engagement 
  • Continuous Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition | SAP Community

Temporary Workaround: Building a Custom API

While the CIP request works its way through the process, partners should not be left idle. Custom APIs provide a viable bridge. Two options are available as mentioned below.

Option 1: Custom CDS View Exposed as an External API

This is the preferred no-code/low-code approach that uses standard S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition on stack key user extensibility — no separate ABAP environment required.

Step 1 — Identify Released CDS Views Open the View Browser App in S/4HANA Cloud and locate released CDS views that can serve as the data source for your required API.

Step 2 — Create a Custom CDS View

  • Open the Custom CDS View App.
  • Select the relevant released CDS view(s) as the data source.
  • Add required fields, maintain field properties, and publish the Custom CDS View with the External API setting enabled.
  • Demo video - Creating Custom CDS Views as External APIs - SAP S/4HANA Cloud Extensibility

Step 3 — Expose via a Communication Scenario

  • Open the Custom Communication Scenario App and create a new Custom Communication Scenario.
  • Add the published Custom CDS View (External API) to the scenario and publish it.
  • Create a Communication Arrangement:
    • Assign the Custom Communication Scenario to the arrangement.
    • Create or maintain the Communication System and Communication User.
    • Activate the arrangement and copy the Service URL for testing.
  • Demo Video - Exposing Custom CDS Views as External APIs - SAP S/4HANA Cloud Extensibility

Step 4 — Test the Custom API Validate the endpoint using Postman or any API testing tool against the copied Service URL.

Note: The custom API's is a custom artifact created using above steps would allow Read-Only operation and would not support Create Update and Delete operations.

Option 2: RAP - Based API (ABAP Development)

For partners with access to an ABAP development environment — either BTP ABAP Environment or an S/4HANA Cloud development tenant — a RESTful ABAP Programming model (RAP) offers greater flexibility.

  1. Develop a RAP-based custom API using ABAP Development Tools (ADT).
  2. Release the custom API for ABAP Cloud consumption, making it a custom public API.
  3. Activate the released API via Communication Arrangements in the target tenant.

Custom API Delivery Approaches

Once a Custom API is built, partners need to decide how to deliver it — especially for multi-customer scenarios:

 

ApproachDescriptionBest Suited For
Multi Off (Multi-Customer Off-Stack)Package the custom API as part of an on-stack customization delivered via gCTS (Git-enabled Change and Transport System)Partners delivering solutions to few customers.
Scalable (Cross-Stack Extension)Combine an on-stack add-on (custom API on S/4HANA) with a side-by-side BTP extension that consumes the API.Packaged ABAP Cloud AddOn delivered  to customer via SAP Store using Landscape Portal.

Current Known Facts:

It would be remiss not to highlight the gaps that currently constrain these workarounds:

  1. Read-Only Operations Only: Custom APIs currently support only READ (GET) operations. Create, Update, and Delete (CUD) operations are not supported. This works as designed since CDS views are released for Readonly operation.

  2. Unreleased CDS Views: Not all CDS views have been released for custom use. This directly blocks Option 1 for certain data objects, forcing partners toward the more complex RAP-based approach or leaving them temporarily without a viable workaround. in such cases please follow CIP request approach.

  3. On-Stack Dependency for Multi-Tenant SaaS: Partners building multi-tenant SaaS applications that consume Custom APIs are required to deliver an on-stack extension component — adding architectural complexity and incremental cost to their delivery model. This works as designed since its a Cross Stack custom solution.

Summary and Recommended Actions

Here is a consolidated view of what partners should do today:

 

Area Recommended Action
CIP SubmissionCheck CIP campaigns 1175 (Remote) and 2759 (Local) — vote on existing requests or submit new ones.
Custom APIsUse Custom CDS Views (Option 1) or RAP wrappers (Option 2) as an interim workaround while CIP requests are processed.
CUD OperationsFlag any use cases requiring Create/Update/Delete operations — escalate via partner support if this is a project blocker.
CDS View GapsIf Option 1 is blocked due to an unreleased CDS view, submit via CIP Campaign 2759 and request fast-track review.
Multi-Tenant ArchitectureEngage with SAP Architecture / Partner Reference Applications (PRA) teams for guidance on on-stack add-on and cross-stack delivery models.

Closing Thoughts

Missing Public APIs need not be a dead-end for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition implementations. The path forward is clear: use the SAP Customer Influence Programme as the permanent vehicle for getting APIs officially released, and leverage Custom APIs as a structured, supported interim solution.

The combination of partner advocacy through CIP voting, tactical Custom API development, and SAP's roadmap commitments around CRUD support and CDS view releases should collectively close the gap — both today and over the coming release cycles.

If you have encountered similar challenges in your own S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition projects, consider voting on the relevant CIP campaigns and sharing your use case — your input directly shapes the product roadmap.

Key Reference Links

  • Overview | SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition | SAP Business Accelerator Hub
  • Remote APIs — CIP Campaign: https://influence.sap.com/sap/ino/#/campaign/1175
  • Local APIs — CIP Campaign : https://influence.sap.com/sap/ino/#/campaign/2759
  • SAP Community Blog Post - New Guided Missions for SAP Partners: Build Once. Scale to Many
  • Build Solutions for SAP Cloud ERP with confidence - SAP Community

This blog post is based on guidance current as of 2026. The CRUD operation gap and unreleased CDS view limitations are actively tracked as product improvement items.

entry.title: Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub
entry.content:
One of the key benefits of making Event APIs available through SAP Developer Hub is enabling a self-service experience for developers. Whether they are internal developers or external developers and business partners, they can discover Event API Products, subscribe to it, and use the credentials provided by the Developer Hub to consume the events themselves or publish events.

This blog is Part 4 of a four-part series, covering the journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to consuming Event APIs through Developer Hub:

  1. Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
  2. Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
  3. Part 3: Publishing event APIs on Developer Hub and managing API Products
  4. Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

You don't need to have followed the previous parts to complete this tutorial. In this part, we’ll take the perspective of a developer using Developer Hub: we’ll discover an Event API Product, subscribe to it, retrieve the required credentials, and use them to connect to the Event Broker and consume events.

We'll cover the following:

  • Before you start (prerequisites):
  • Event API Products: Discover and Subscribe
  • Event APIs: Publishing and Consuming
  • What's next

Before you start (prerequisites):

  1. Be onboarded as an Application Developer in the Developer Hub.
  2. Have access to a client where you can test the connectivity to the Event Broker, in this example I'm using the "Try Me!" in SAP Integration Suite, Advanced Event Mesh
  3. Optionally: Have viewing rights to the Event Portal and Application Domain in your Advanced Event Mesh environment

Event API Products: Discover and Subscribe 

  1. Go to the home page of the Developer Hub and go to your API Product containing event APIs.

     

  2. Under "Events", you see an overview of the event APIs that are part of this product. "Rate Plan" gives you details on the rate plan that is linked to it the event API Product (defines messaging type, access type, queue type, etc.), "Associated Subscriptions" list which applications are subscribed to this Event API Product. Feel free to browse these different tabs.
  3. Now, let's subscribe to the Event API Product, click on the button "Subscribe" on the right top and create the application (either create a new subscription or add it to an existing API application). 

  4. If you're creating a new API Application, enter a name (e.g. Sales Order Application) and optionally a short text and a description and press "Create". 

     

  5. Once you created the application, you will be automatically redirected to the application. Later, you can find the application in the Developer Hub under "My Workspace". 
  6. In the application, you will find the credentials you can use to authenticate to the event broker/event API. "Key" will serve as your username and "Secret" as your password. For this tutorial, copy these credentials. 

     

  7. When consuming events using guaranteed messaging, the application consumes them from a queue. This allows messages to be stored on Advanced Event Mesh if the application is temporarily unavailable or cannot process messages as quickly as they are generated. In this case, you will also need the name of your queue, you find this in your application by going to "Products", select your Event API Product, under "Queue Details" you find the name of your queue. Also copy the name of the queue for this tutorial.

     

  8. Optionally: if you have access to the event portal in Advanced Event Mesh (optional), you will see that after the creation of an application in the Developer Hub a new application is created in your Application Domain.

     

Event APIs: Publishing and Consuming

For publishing events to and/or consuming events from Event APIs using your credentials from the Developer Hub, you can use any client as long as you are able to specifcy the following:

  • Broker URL (e.g.  https://mr-connection-xxxxx.messaging.solace.cloud:9443)
  • Message VPN 
  • Client Username (key copied from Developer Hub)
  • Client Password (secret copied from Developer Hub)
  • Queue Name (name copied from Developer Hub)
  • Topic (found in the Async API spec on the Developer Hub)

Make sure your Queue Name and Topic are in line with the documentation. The key and secret provided are only whitelisted for the topics and queues that are part of the Event API Products in your API Application. If you try to subscribe or publish to a topic that is not included in the API Product, the operation will fail.

⚠️If you don't know which Broker URL or Message VPN should be used, reach out to one of your administrators in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh.

To demonstrate how the connection works, I will use "Try Me!" in Advanced Event Mesh.

  1. In SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, go to "Cluster Manager" ➡️ select your Broker Service ➡️ click on "Try Me!" and at the left bottom of the page, hit "Open Broker Manager".
  2. In "Try Me!", enter the following under "Publisher":
    • Broker URL (e.g.  https://mr-connection-xxxxx.messaging.solace.cloud:9443)
    • Message VPN 
    • Client Username (key copied from Developer Hub)
    • Client Password (secret copied from Developer Hub)
  3. Make sure under "Subscriber" you checked "✅ Same as Publisher"
  4. Hit "Connect" at both the "Publisher" as the "Subscriber" side.
  5. You should now see the word "Connected" under "Establish Connections". 

     

  6. Once the connection is established, scroll down to "Bind to an endpoint to receive guaranteed messages" on the "Subscriber" side:
    1. Select "Queue"
    2. Enter the queue name copied from the Developer Hub
    3. Hit "Start Consume"
    4. You should now see that the consumer is active

       

  7. If you were able to subscribe to the queue, scroll down to "Publish to topic" on the "Publisher" side:
    1. Enter the topic you want to publish on (needs to be part of an Event API Product where your API Application is subscribed to)
    2. Delivery Mode can remain "Direct"
    3. Enter a payload under "Message Content"
    4. Hit "Publish"
  8. After publishing events on the topic, you should see the messages appearing on the right side of the page (under "Subscriber"). This means that the messages are successfully being published on the topic and landing in the queue, using the credentials generated by creating an API Application. 

     

What's next 

You’ve now seen how developers can discover, subscribe to, and consume Event APIs through SAP Developer Hub using a self-service approach.

This concludes our journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to enabling a self-service experience for developers to consume Event APIs through Developer Hub.

If you want to see the complete picture and how the different pieces fit together, head back to the main blog, which provides an overview of the full series.

entry.title: Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
entry.content:
To bring Event APIs from SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh into the familiar API developer experience of SAP Developer Hub, Advanced Event Mesh first needs to be enabled for API Management.

This blog is Part 1 of a four-part series, covering the journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to consuming Event APIs through Developer Hub:

  1. Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
  2. Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
  3. Part 3: Publishing event APIs on Developer Hub and managing API Products
  4. Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

In this first part, we’ll focus on the required setup to enable Advanced Event Mesh for API Management and prepare the environment for the next steps.
Note that in the example we only use 1 broker, if you are using multiple brokers you need to repeat the steps for these brokers as well.

Prerequisites

Before going through this tutorial, we strongly recommend you already have created:

  • a Service in the Cluster Manager
  •  a Modeled Event Mesh in the Runtime Event Manager (containing at least 1 Broker)

The roles required in SAP AEM for this tutorial are:

  • Mission Control Manager
  • Event Portal Administrator 

On your workstation:

  • Terraform CLI Client 
    ℹ️     Don't worry, you don't need any prior Terraform experience.
    That said, some Terraform knowledge can come in handy when troubleshooting. 

Enable Event Broker connections on your event mesh

First, we need to get the endpoint of the broker where you want to enable API connectivity. This is what we'll use in the Runtime Event Manager to enable the connectivity itself.

  1. In the Cloud Console of SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, go to "Cluster Manager"

     

  2. Go to the the Event Broker where you want to enable API connectivity.

     

  3. Press "Connect", select a Client Library such as "REST", and copy the host
    ⚠️Note: you don't need to copy the protocol (e.g. https) or the port (e.g. 9443), what you copied should be in the following format: ########.messaging.solace.cloud or 123.89.40.72
  4. Once you copied the host, go to "Runtime Event Manager" to enable the connectivity.
  5.  Select the modeled event mesh where you want to enable the API connectivity

     

  6. Click on "Event Broker Connections", select the Event Broker where you want to enable API connectivity and press "View Connection Details"

     

  7. Paste the host under "Host".
    ⚠️make sure you don't have the protocol or port in here!
  8. Add the protocols you need (e.g. REST, SMF, AMQP) by clicking on "Add Protocols".
    You can change transport (e.g. https instead of http) and port settings once you selected your preferred protocol(s).
    For this tutorial I kept the default settings as-is, I just enabled secure transport. The authentication should remain "Basic Authentication".

     

Add predefined client profiles to your Event Broker

Before an Event API Product can be used on an event broker, API Management expects a specific set of six client profiles to already exist on that broker. When an application is approved against a plan, APIM assigns it a client username and picks one of these profiles based on what the plan allows. If the profiles aren't there, that assignment has nothing to point at and application will not work properly.

The six cover the combinations of guaranteed messaging permissions a plan can grant:

Client ProfileGuaranteed Messaging
APIM-NoGMnone - direct messaging only
APIM-ReceiveOnlyGMreceive
APIM-SendOnlyGMsend
APIM-ReceiveSendGMsend + receive
APIM-ReceiveCreateEndpGMreceive + create endpoints
APIM-ReceiveSendCreateEndpGMsend + receive + create endpoints

You could click all six into Broker Manager by hand. But Advanced Event Mesh can be managed via SEMP APIs/Terraform, so let's discover that. There is a Terraform project published on Github that creates the client profiles declaratively, that's what we'll use here. It takes about ten minutes from a standing start, including installing Terraform. More information can be found in the documentation.

  1. Go back to the Event Broker where you want to enable API connectivity (under to "Cluster Manager").

  2. Go to "Connect", go to the bottom and press "SEMP - REST API".
  3. Under "SEMP Credentials", select "Mission Control Manager" (also works with other users as long as it is an admin user), copy the following details and paste it into a notepad:
    • SEMP Public Endpoint (e.g. https://mr-connection-xxxxxx.messaging.solace.cloud:943)
    • Message VPN
    • Username (in this example: mission-control-manager)
    • Password

       


  4. Now, let's use Terraform!
    Open your terminal and to install Homebrew and Terraform, using the following commands one by one (optional, skip if you already have Terraform)
brew tap hashicorp/tap
brew install hashicorp/tap/terraform
terraform -version​

Note: if a Terraform version appears after executing "terraform -version" (e.g. Terraform v1.16.1) the installation of Terraform was successful

  • Use the command line to navigate to the folder where you want to keep the Terraform project (command: cd), and clone the following Git Repository.
git clone https://github.com/solace-cto-labs/terraform-solacebroker-apim-clientprofiles.git
cd terraform-solacebroker-apim-clientprofiles

The project contains 3 files: "providers.tf" names the provider plugin, "variables.tf" contains the inputs, and "main.tf" declares the six client profiles. If you have a look at these files, it is very readable even if you've never seen Terraform.

  • Create a file and name the file "terraform.tfvars", this will contain the values of the variables. This should contain the following:
url          = "https://mr-connection-xxxx.messaging.solace.cloud:943"
msg_vpn_name = "my-service-vpn"
username     = "mgmt-user"​​

⚠️Don't forget to replace the variables in the file with your own url, VPN name and username copied from step 3.

  • Now, go back to the terminal (in folder "terraform-solacebroker-apim-clientprofiles"). In the previous step, we didn't put the password in the file, this we did on purpose. Pass the password as an environment variable using the following command:
export TF_VAR_password='your-management-password'​
  • Let's download the provider plugind:
terraform init​
  • Execute the following command, this reads your broker over SEMP, compares it to the configuration, and prints what it would do without changing anything:
terraform plan​
  • When everything worked fine so far, you can execute the terraform apply command.
terraform apply​

  • It shows the plan again and waits. Type "yes" in full.

  • You should now see that the terraform was applied, for example:
    Apply complete! Resources: 6 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

     
  • You can verify in the cloud console whether the profiles have been added, go to Cluster Manager ➡️ select your Broker ➡️ click on "Open Broker Manager" on the right top.

     

  • Now, go to Access Control ➡️ Client Profiles. You should see the 6 new profiles being listed here.

     

What's next

If you were able to enable the connectivity on your event broker in the Runtime Event Manager and you have added the 6 client profiles: congratulations you have finished part 1 of this blog series and prepared Advanced Event Mesh for integration with API Management.

With this foundation in place, we can now move on to
Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub.

entry.title: Part 3: Publishing Event APIs in Developer Hub and Managing API Products
entry.content:
Introduction

With Advanced Event Mesh connected to Developer Hub, we can make our Event APIs available to developers and allow them to subscribe to them.

This blog is Part 3 of a four-part series, covering the journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to consuming Event APIs through Developer Hub:

  1. Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
  2. Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
  3. Part 3: Publishing Event APIs in Developer Hub and Managing API Products
  4. Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

In this part, we’ll create and release an Event API in Advanced Event Mesh, publish it as an API Product through Developer Hub, and show you how you can configure that product.

We'll cover the following:

  • Introduction
  • Before you start (prerequisites):
  • Make Event APIs available for Developer Hub
  • Publish an API Product
  • Configure the API Product
  • What's next


Before you start (prerequisites):

  1. Have the Event Portal Administrator role assigned to you in an Advanced Event Mesh instance
    (we’ll be managing Event Portal objects)
  2. Have the “AuthGroup.Content.Admin” role collection assigned to you in subaccount where your SAP Integration Suite tenant is running
  3. Be onboarded as an Application Developer in the Developer Hub.

Make Event APIs available for Developer Hub

In order to make events visible from on the Developer Hub, the event APIs (and all related objects like event and schema) need to be in the “Released” state. If event APIs are not shared, you will still see it in the Developer Hub, but you will not be able to add it to an API Product. Adding an Event API to an API Product is crucial for subscribing to the event API. So, in this part of the tutorial we will make an event API, share it and release it.

  1. Let’s make an Event API, go to Advanced Event Mesh and go to the "Designer".

     

  2. Select the Application Domain where you want to expose the event API from.
    In this example we’ll release a SalesOrder API which is part of the domain “Customer Experience”.

     

  3. Select the table view at left top ➡️ go to “Event APIs” and click “Create Event API”
  4. Enter a name e.g. “Sales Order Events” and enter the following details:
    • Broker Type: Solace
    • Allow Event API to be shared across application domains ➡️ Check ✅!
    • Version Name & Description are optional

       

  5. Scroll down to "Event Flows" and click on “Manage Event APIs”, look for the events you want to make be part of your event API and select whether you want it the API to enable publishing or subscribing (or both) to this event. In this example, I will add all sales order events for both pub and sub.


  6. Once you selected the events, close the “Manage Events” tab and click on “Save Event API” at the right bottom.

     

  7. Now, let’s change the state of the event API to “Released”. In order to do so, all objects related this event need to be in “Released” state. Go back to your event API, click on the 3 dots next to one of the events and click on “Open Event”.

     

  8. Here you’ll see the details of the event, including the schema. If the event schema is not in “Released” state, click on the 3 dots right next to the schema and click on “Open Schema”.

     

  9. In the schema, make sure your version is according to your own guidelines, then click on “Manage Lifecycle”.

     

  10. A pop-up appears, in the drop down box choose “Released” and press “Save”.
    You should see the state of the schema is now “Released”. 

     

  11. Now, go back to your event. Make sure your versioning is according to your own guidelines in the event, click “Manage Lifecycle” as well and also change the state to “Released” and press “Save”.
    In the event, you should now see that both your event and schema are released.

     

  12. Close the tab and repeat this for all events in your event API.
  13. Once all events “Released”, click on “Manage Lifecycle” in your event API and also release the event API. Your event API should look similar to the screenshot below with all events and the event API itself in “Released” state and the Event API Details should mention “Shared”.

     

Publish an API Product

If you have successfully connected the Developer Hub with SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, you have created an event API and now want to make it discoverable for internal or external developers and allow them to subscribe to the event API, you have to add this an API Product. Before creating an API Product, we will be creating an event rate plan. This rate plan defines the messaging type, access type, queue type, and other configurations that control how events are delivered to consumers. More info on event rate plans can be found in the documentation.

  1. Go to SAP Integration Suite ➡️ Developer Hub ➡️ Admin Center ➡️ Content ➡️ Rate Plans

  2. Under "Rate Plans", click "Create".


  3. Enter a unique name, select a messaging type, access type and queue type and define a maximum time-to-live & spool size and press "Create".

     

  4. Now, we are going to create the Event API Product. Go to "Business Systems", select the SAP AEM Business System we created in Part 2.

     

  5. Click on the Application Domain where you want to expose the event API from (e.g. Customer Experience). Here you should see the event API.


  6. If you click on the event API, you should see the event reference.
  7. Now close the event API.

     

  8. This will take you back to the overview of your event APIs for this application domain. If you select your application domain, you can click on “Create product”.
  9. Enter the product details and hit "Next".
     
  10. Select the rate plan we just created and click "Next".

     

  11. Select the broker where you want to enable deploy the API Product, application and queue to. 
  12. Choose the supported protocols, and click "Next".

  13. Now, you see an overview of the API Product you want to create, if everything looks fine, just click "Publish".

     

  14. A pop-up appears explaining that the request to publish this product has been created. If you want to check the status or finalize the publication of your API product, go to on “Scheduled Requests”.

     

  15. Once published, go to the home page of the Developer Hub, you should see that the API Product has been added.

     

Configure the API Product

  1. In the Developer Hub, go to Admin Center  Content.
  2. Click on “Products” and select your API Product, from here you can edit, unpublish and/or remove the product or alter permissions.

     

What's next

We’ve now released an Event API and published it as an API Product in Developer Hub, making it available for developers to discover and subscribe to.

In Part 4, we’ll complete the journey by subscribing to an Event API from Developer Hub and consuming the events:
Part 4: Consuming Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

entry.title: Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
entry.content:
With Advanced Event Mesh enabled for API Management (covered in Part 1 of this blog series), we can now connect it to SAP Developer Hub and make the Event APIs available through the familiar developer experience.

This blog is Part 2 of a four-part series, covering the journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to consuming Event APIs through Developer Hub:

  1. Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
  2. Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
  3. Part 3: Publishing Event APIs in Developer Hub and Managing API Products
  4. Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

In this part, we’ll create the required API token in Advanced Event Mesh and use it to establish a connection to Developer Hub in SAP Integration Suite.

Before you start (prerequisites):

  1. Have the Administrator role assigned to you in an Advanced Event Mesh instance
    (we’ll be creating a token and managing Event Portal objects)
  2. Have the “AuthGroup.Content.Admin” role collection assigned to you in subaccount where your SAP Integration Suite tenant is running
  3. Have the “Destination Administrator” role collection assigned to you in the subaccount where your SAP Integration Suite tenant is running

Creating an API Token

First, we need to create an API Token in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh. This API Token will get the right permissions and will be used for authentication by the Developer Hub while connecting to Advanced Event Mesh.

  1. Go to the cloud console of SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, copy the base URL of your tenant
    (e.g. https://eu20.console.pubsub.em.services.cloud.sap) 
    ⚠️don't forget to copy "https://"
  2. Click on the user icon at the left bottom ➡️ go to “Token Management”
  3. Click on “Create Token”
  4. Enter a name for your token, your API token must have at least the following permissions:
    PermissionsAPI Token Permission
    Allow access to Mission Controlmission_control:access
    Get My Services with Management Credentialsservices:get:self
    Create/Update/Delete Client Profilesservice_requests:post:client_profile
    Get Services with Management Credentialsservices:get
    Read any Applicationapplication:get:*
    Read any Application Domainapplication_domain:get:*
    Do anything to any Event APIevent_api:*:*
    Do anything to any Event API Productevent_api_product:*:*
    Access to Event Portal Designerevent_designer:access
    Get Application Configuration Pushapplication_configuration_push_job:get:*
    Get Environment in Event Portalep_environment:get:*
    Get Event Broker in Event Portalmodeled_event_broker:get:*
    Get Modeled Event Mesh in Event Portalmodeled_event_mesh:get:*
    Create, update, or delete published event API products and their underlaying resourcesapim_event_api_product:*:*
    Get published event API products and their underlaying resourcesapim_event_api_product:get:*
  5. Once the right permissions are selected, click on "Create Token".

     

  6. Now, a pop-up with the API Token appears.
    ⚠️It's is important you copy this token and keep it for the next steps. Once the pop-up is closed you cannot reaccess the API token for security reasons. If you lose it, you’ll have to regenerate the token.

  7. After closing the pop-up, click on the 3 dots at the right side of the token you just created and select “View Token”.

     

  8. Copy the Token ID from the token details.

    ✅If you have the Base URL of your AEM Cloud Console, your API Token and your Token ID at hand you are ready for the next part in this tutorial.

Create a destination on SAP BTP

After creating an API Token in Advanced Event Mesh, we’ll create a destination from the subaccount where the SAP Integration Suite is running. This destination will be used by the Developer Hub to connect to Advanced Event Mesh.

  1. Go to your subaccount ➡️ under “Connectivity”, select “Destinations” ➡️ click on “Create” ➡️ and select “Create New Destination From Scratch”
  2. Give the destination and a name and description and enter the following details:
    • Type: HTTP
    • Proxy Type: Internet
    • URL: [AEM Base URL, copied in step 1 of the previous sections]
    • User: Token ID
    • Password: API Token
    • Additional Properties:
      • Key: sap.isuite.dh.aem.enabled
      • Value: true

         

  3. After you created the destination, you can validate whether everything works fine by clicking on "Check connection" and in Developer Hub. Go to SAP Integration Suite  click on the 9 little dots you see on the right top ➡️ go to “Developer Hub”

     

  4. In the Developer Hub, go to “Admin Center” ➡️ click on “Content”.
  5. Here you should see your Advanced Event Mesh environment under “Business Systems”, the name and description in the table should be the same name and description as your destination. Click on your AEM system.

     

  6. You should see the all your Application Domains being listed. Clicking on the Application Domain, you should see all events available in this domain. If you don’t see any events here, continue this tutorial, it will explain you how to get your Event APIs being published. If you already see some event APIs being there, skip to section "Publish an API Product".
    If you haven't created any Application Domain yet (with applications, schemas and events), please do so, this will be required for the following exercises.

     

What's next

If you see your Application Domains (from AEM) appearing in the Developer Hub it means we’ve now connected Advanced Event Mesh with Developer Hub.

In the next part, we’ll take the next step by publishing Event APIs in Developer Hub and creating and managing the API Products that make them available to developers: 
Part 3: Publishing event APIs on Developer Hub and managing API Products.

entry.title: Building and Consuming an MCP Server in SAP Integration Suite - Connecting it to Claude and Joule
entry.content:
Introduction

In this blog, I want to share my hands-on experience of building an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server in SAP Integration Suite, and then consuming it from two different AI agents - Claude and Joule. I explored this end-to-end, from the initial setup and configuration challenges to the final working agents, and I am documenting the journey here in case it helps others attempting the same thing.

Prerequisites

Before you start creating API and MCP artifacts in Integration Suite, make sure the following are in place:

  1. Cloud Integration and API Management capabilities are activated in Integration Suite.
  2. The Integration Cell runtime is enabled - go to Settings → Runtimes and confirm it shows Active. The MCP Server artifact runs on Integration Cell, it cannot be deployed to the classic Cloud Integration runtime.
  3. Your service plan is Premium or Enhanced edition - MCP is available only in the Premium and Enhanced edition plans
  4. The PI_Integration_Developer role collection is assigned to your user in the BTP Cockpit.

Architecture

Here's the high-level flow I used to connect Claude and Joule to Integration Suite via the MCP server:

                Joule / Claude
                      |
   Claude Connector / Joule Destination
   (connection via Developer Hub or BTP OAuth credentials)
                      |
               MCP Server artifact
                      |
           (accesses API artifacts)
                      |
  API Artifact (Integration Suite OData APIs /
                    CPI iFlows)
                      |
               API response
                      |
            Back to Claude / Joule

I have split this blog into two parts. first, creating the MCP server in Integration Suite, and second, connecting it separately to Claude and to Joule. The MCP server itself stays the same in both scenarios, only the connection method changes.

For the examples in this blog, I used two inputs to build the API specification, the standard Integration Suite OData APIs, and a plain iFlow consumed through the MCP server.

Part 1: Creating the MCP Server in Integration Suite

Step 1: Creating the API Artifact

An MCP artifact can be created in a couple of ways in Integration Suite:

  • Option 1: Create an API artifact by uploading an OpenAPI 3.0 specification, then deploy it to the Integration Cell runtime.
  • Option 2: Configure the target URL directly and build the API specification inside the MCP artifact itself.

I went with Option 1, using the standard Integration Suite OData API as my example.

 

 

1.1 Creating the API Artifact

In an Integration Suite package, I created an API artifact with the Runtime profile set to Integration Cell.

 

 

Under Select API type, I chose URL or Specification, and within that, OData - since the MCP server was going to consume a standard Integration Suite OData service. There are other options too: REST (useful for posting data to an iFlow or a third-party API) and SOAP, if SOAP services are involved.

 

 

 

 

Note: Use OData if your API artifact relies purely on OData APIs. If it's a mix of OData and iFlow calls, go with REST instead - OData can still be reached via the HTTP adapter within a REST based API artifact.

The next important step is preparing the API specification to upload into the API artifact. I used the YAML file from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub to generate my API specification.

 

 

 
Note: The JSON/YAML file from SAP Business Accelerator Hub is in Swagger 2.0 format, but the MCP server expects the specification in OpenAPI 3.0. You can convert it using an online tool - I used the Swagger Editor and its converter  or alternatively, use the API artifact's "create" option to generate a spec from prompts.

 

 
Once the spec was uploaded with the endpoint details, I validated it inside the API artifact. The spec I used contained the standard CPI OData APIs.

 

 

 
From there, I navigated to the Policy section and configured the OData adapter with the required credentials deployed in the security material, everything else stayed unchanged. Under Authentication, the api.invoke scope is present by default, but you can add your own scope if needed. Make sure Trust Upstream MCP Authorization is enabled.
 
 

 

 
I then deployed the API artifact after completing this configuration.

 

Step 2: Creating the MCP Server

With the API artifact deployed, I created the MCP server on top of it.

 

 

I selected the MCP artifact and chose API as the Source type, since I already had an API artifact created. (There's also an HTTP endpoint option if you want to bypass the API artifact step entirely.)

 

 
Under Provide MCP details, I selected the API artifact I had created and provided a unique path under MCP path.

 

 

 

Once created, the MCP server picks up the tools from the API artifact, I made sure all tools were available in the MCP artifact.

 

  

Important configuration step: under the MCP artifact's Policy, the authentication parameter is OAuth with Client Certificate (not modifiable). In the Authorization policy setting, you choose between:

  • OAuth scope — for connecting the MCP server using BTP integration flow credentials.
  • Developer key — for connecting the MCP server using Developer Hub credentials.

 

 
The HTTP adapter configuration didn't need any changes - it still points to the API artifact I created.
 
 
I deployed the MCP artifact and confirmed its status under Manage Integration Content, in the Integration Cell runtime.
 
With that, the MCP server itself was ready. The next steps cover how I connected this MCP server to Claude, and separately, to Joule.

 

Part 2: Connecting the MCP Server to Claude

Claude uses a redirect mechanism to connect to an MCP server, so the traditional BTP OAuth credentials alone aren't sufficient here. I used the Developer Hub method instead to connect the MCP server to Claude.

Steps I followed

  1. In the Developer Hub, under Admin Center, I navigated to Content.

 

           
 
        2. I clicked on Business System, where all the deployed API and MCP servers are listed.
 
              

              

 

              

 

         3. I selected the required MCP server and created a Product from it.

 

 

              

 

               

        4. I navigated to the newly created product and created a new Subscription for it.

 

               
 
         5. I provided a name and short text for the agent. The key part here is configuring the Claude URL in the Callback URL field -                 this is what allows Claude to authenticate against the MCP server.

 

 
                

 

Once the agent was created, I could see the Token URL along with the ID and Secret.

 

 
Adding the CPI MCP server to Claude
  1. In Claude, I navigated to Customize → Connectors → Add Custom Connector.    

 

            

        2. I provided a name and the MCP server URL (from Integration Suite), then clicked Continue.

 

              
 
          3. Under Authentication, I selected Always Required, and under OAuth Client, I chose Use your own OAuth client, then clicked                Add.

 

                
 
Once authentication succeeded, all the tools inside the MCP server became visible in Claude. By default, tools show as Needs Approval - I changed the status to Approved for the tools I wanted to test and use (you can also approve all of them at once).

 

 

 

I have shared a few results below from testing this in Claude - the responses were genuinely impressive.

 

 

 

Part 3: Connecting the MCP Server to Joule

I connected Joule to CPI in two different ways:

  1. By creating a Skill and Action that uses a CPI iFlow to make the required API calls and respond to Joule (essentially, straightforward iFlow execution).
  2. By consuming the CPI MCP server directly inside a Joule agent, providing instructions and an LLM model, and then deploying it to an environment.

Here is how I connected the CPI MCP server to Joule using the second approach:

  1. For Claude, I used the Developer Hub method — but for Joule, I used BTP OAuth credentials (the integration flow credentials, not the API ones). In the BTP Cockpit, I navigated to my Build subaccount, then Connectivity → Destinations, and created a destination with only the host name — no path prefix, since that gets provided inside the Joule agent itself. I configured the destination with OAuth details, and added these additional properties:
    • sap-joule-studio-mcp-server = true
    • sap.processautomation.enabled = true
    • sap.mcp.tools.enabled = true
  2. I repeated the same setup in the Joule subaccount.
    Note: The destination must exist in both subaccounts, with the same name and the same properties.
  3. For each destination, in both subaccounts, I clicked Check Connection to confirm it was healthy.
  4. Once the destination was created, I went to SAP Build → Control Tower → Destination and confirmed it was available there too.

     

     

  5. Next, I created an agent in Joule to consume the CPI MCP server. In the Build lobby, I clicked Create and selected Joule Skill/Agent.

     

  6. I provided a name and description to proceed, and once the project was created, clicked Create again to build the Joule agent itself.
 
 

 

              

 

              
 
         7. I provided a name, identifier, and description. (Worth noting: Joule uses every detail you provide here when executing a task,               so it's worth being thorough.)

 

 
               
 
          8. Inside the Joule agent, I provided the Expertise and Instructions in detail, so the agent would behave correctly based on my                prompts, and selected the model settings to fit my needs.

 

                
                
 
            9. Under MCP servers, I clicked Add MCP server, gave it a unique name and description, and under the Advanced tab,                                provided the MCP server path (the same Integration Cell host name used in the destination) and selected the destination I                  had created.

 

 
                        
 
               10. After adding it, I clicked Refresh Tools, which pulled in and displayed all the tools available inside the MCP server.

 

 
                      
 
As a final step, I set the agent output format to Markdown so Joule could render the output cleanly. Once everything was configured, I saved the agent and deployed it to an environment (environments can be created under Control Tower → Environment). Additional tools can be added to this agent if required
 
 
With that, the MCP server was live and usable from both Claude and Joule. Provided the Joule results in Business use case section

Business Use Cases I Built With This

1. CPI Monitoring Agent

As shown throughout this blog, this agent uses the standard Integration Suite OData APIs to pull monitoring information based on user queries. I have handed this over to the support team and business admins so they can retrieve monitoring information and perform a few admin tasks directly, without needing to log into Integration Suite.

2. SuccessFactors Agent

I am currently working on an ongoing SuccessFactors implementation project that integrates with multiple systems - Concur, Active Directory, SAP, Staffbase, and others. As the project entered the SIT phase, the functional team needed support from the CPI team to run ad-hoc flows. I built this agent so the functional team could run the entire testing process from Joule itself, without involving the CPI team each time.

For example: the user tells Joule which interface they want to run, and Joule suggests the required inputs (filter type and value). Once the user provides that input, an API call goes to the CPI iFlow, which executes the transaction, fetches the monitoring report based on the correlation ID, and returns the monitoring status directly in Joule - completing the whole loop.

 

 

 

What I found elegant about this agent is that the inputs can be very user-friendly. Users only need to specify the interface and filter type they want, for instance, entering a date like "25th Aug" for a last-modified-date filter and the API specification takes care of formatting it correctly.

3. IDoc Reprocessing Agent

This agent works from both Claude and Joule. The user provides a date range, and the agent retrieves IDoc failures from SAP (via WE02) through an OData call routed through the MCP server. (By default, the OData request attempts to reprocess the IDoc in SAP first — only IDocs that still fail after reprocessing show up as failures in CPI.) For genuine failures, the agent creates a ServiceNow request and reports everything back to the user.

Challenges I Faced

  1. Connecting the CPI MCP server to Claude — in my initial attempts, the redirect URL wasn't configured, and it wasn't clear how to do it. I eventually got Claude's redirect URL and configured it in the Developer Hub.
  2. Setting up authentication via Developer Hub — the full configuration process wasn't clear at first, and took some trial and error to get right.
  3. Choosing the right authorization policy inside the MCP artifact — for Joule versus Claude. The api.invoke role is meant for Developer Hub credentials, while ESBMessaging.send (or any custom role) works for BTP OAuth credentials. To use BTP OAuth, you need to select the OAuth scope or developer key option under Authorization Type.
  4. Defining the API specification — for the CPI agent, I used the standard Integration Suite OData JSON/YAML files, which come in Swagger 2.0 by default, while the API artifact expects OpenAPI 3.0. Getting the conversion and customization right took some care.
  5. Handling multiple target URLs for the SuccessFactors agent — I needed to call a CPI iFlow for posting data, and OData APIs for fetching monitoring logs, which meant defining two target URLs in the API specification. I solved this inside the API artifact policy using a router. The tricky part was figuring out what payload was coming into the iFlow, since there's no built-in trace option — I ended up using debug mode and found the API path coming through in the header, which I then used to route to the correct URL.
  6. Getting the Joule destination right — the host name of the MCP server (Integration Cell) needs to be provided during destination creation, along with the OAuth credentials, and the three additional properties (sap-joule-studio-mcp-server, sap.processautomation.enabled, sap.mcp.tools.enabled) all need to be set to true.

Claude vs. Joule: What I Learned

To be clear, this isn't a comparison of which tool is better,  it's about how each one needs to be configured and used:

  • Joule works more precisely the more detailed instructions you give it while building the agent. Requests from Joule don't go directly against the MCP server's API specification, Joule first checks the instructions you defined, and acts accordingly. Claude, on the other hand, works directly against the API specification and responds based on that.
  • Joule expects a much more detailed API specification. For example, if you want to fetch a monitoring status, you need to explicitly define in the HTTP 200 response how the data should be extracted. Claude doesn't need this level of detail, it's able to understand the response and extract the relevant output on its own.

Joule is always the first choice as it is within the SAP ecosystem, and I am hopeful that Joule Studio 2.0 will bring more capabilities to close this gap further.

Conclusion

That's a summary of how I built an MCP server in SAP Integration Suite and connected it to both Claude and Joule. I hope this is useful to others exploring the same setup, happy to hear feedback, suggestions, or answer any questions in the comments.

entry.title: A closer look to the MCP Server of SAP BTP Integation Suite
entry.content:
1. What is the relationship among MCP Server, AI APP and Large Language Model(LLM)

MCP server is nothing but a special wrap up of SAP interfaces. It does NOT have any intelligence at all.

AI APP is a sort of software program, normally has a user friendly UI developed by python or Rust or C# or Typescript or Javascript etc. which ususally has a user interactive functionalily. The AI APP does NOT have any intelligence. It directly consumes MCP server's service, or it consumes services of LLM.

Large Language Model(LLM) is a component which has artificial intelligence. It can understand human natual language and output result inform of human natual language. Some examples of LLM are, OpenAI GPT series, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude etc.

In general, inside the AI APP, MCP server helps LLM deal with SAP data.

2. How to create a provider based API proxy in the Integration Suite.

Before the creation of MCP Server, a source API proxy in the CPI layer has to be created. This process has not been included in Ashutosh's tutorial. Let me add it here.

Let's take the OData v2 API Product as an example. (OData v4 is technically feasible. However its catelog service is not supported by the BTP API Management and it makes the process more complex.)

2.1 configure a provider with catelog service

of course, the cloud connector destination is a prerequiste of this step.

2.2 Import the API in the BTP API Management view

select the API

Download the JSON file from here

runtime profile, choose integration cell

choose the provider configured

click the Add button above, the API proxy will be generated. However it doesn't have any resources. we need to import the json file downloaded last step into it.

switch to the API spec view

 

record this part:

 

then click Edit button beside. then import button

choose the json file and import it.

at first view, the resource structure is in json format.

click button Editor, then click button Code

now use the part backed up to replace this part

this is the updated version

now the API proxy can be saved and deployed. And it should be able to be selected by the MCP Server creation wizard.

 

3. Deal with CSRF-TOKEN

This is my version of the Integration Suite.

Version -4.12.6

Maybe this issue has been fixed by any versions afterwards, anyway in this version , by default the generated OData adapter doesn't support csrf-token. When try to change or create something via the API Proxy, we will get an error saying 

"csrf token validation failed"

Let's fix it here 🙂

add a new receiver to the iflow, then move the odata receiver to this newly added receiver

3.2 Delete the Receiver

when you delete this receiver you will find that the odata receiver has been deleted as well.

before the step 'Request-Reply', add a content modifier.

insert a static http header as below

content-type: application/json; charset=iso-8859-1

now you can save the API proxy and deploy it.

4. Few examples on how to call MCP Server

create a MCP server by choosing the above API proxy

choose tools from the API Proxy resource list

then add this line to the resources

Save and deploy.

step 3. user chooses option 'update product description'

language, new description and product id. This form should be generated based on the user prompt retrieved.

{

        "name": "post_A_Product",
        "arguments": {
            "requestBody": {
                "BaseUnit": "EA",
                "IndustrySector": "I",
                "ProductType": "ROH",
                "to_Description": {
                    "results": [
                        {
                            "Product": "",
                            "Language": "EN",
                            "ProductDescription": "material created by AI"
                        }
                    ]
                }
            }

}

{

entry.title: No-Code MCP Servers with SAP Integration Suite: From REST API to AI Agent
entry.content:
Disclosure: This blog post was written with GenAI assistance. The architecture, implementation choices, and troubleshooting notes are based on hands-on testing.

Introduction

SAP Integration Suite's MCP Gateway exposes managed APIs as MCP Servers — with OAuth 2.0, API policies, and Developer Hub governance — without writing a custom MCP application. This post walks through that flow using the SAP BTP Resource Consumption API as a concrete example.

I previously built a custom Node.js MCP Server on Cloud Foundry for this same API — with application code, XSUAA configuration, a Destination Service, and a CF deployment pipeline. You can read about that approach here:

→ Building an MCP Server to Query SAP BTP Usage Data with AI Assistants

The MCP Gateway in Integration Suite replaces that entire custom application with managed artifacts and policies.

Companion Files

The following files are available in the companion GitHub repository:

File Use

destination.propertiesReady-to-import BTP Destination config — fill in your Client ID, Secret, and Token URL
uas-reporting-oas3-sap-mcp-blog.jsonOpenAPI 3.0.3 spec to upload into the Integration Suite API Artifact
test-mcp.shShell script to validate the MCP Server via curl before connecting an AI agent

Prerequisites

  • SAP BTP account with SAP Integration Suite (Integration Cell runtime active)
  • API Management and Developer Hub enabled
  • Credentials for the SAP BTP Resource Consumption backend
  • Permission to create and deploy API and MCP Server artifacts

Architecture

wo separate auth hops: the agent authenticates to the MCP Server; Integration Suite authenticates to the backend via a BTP Destination. The agent never sees the backend secret.

Step 1 — Create the BTP Destination

In BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Connectivity → Destinations, use Import Destination with the companion destination.properties file, or create it manually:

Name=UAS_Reporting_Destination
Type=HTTP
ProxyType=Internet
URL=https://uas-reporting.cfapps.eu10.hana.ondemand.com
Authentication=OAuth2ClientCredentials

Set Client ID, Client Secret, Token Service URL, and Token Service URL Type = Dedicated.

Add under Labels (not Additional Properties):

IntegrationCell.Include = true

Validate: obtain a token with client_credentials and call the backend directly before continuing:

GET https://uas-reporting.cfapps.eu10.hana.ondemand.com/reports/v1/cloudCreditsDetails

Step 2 — Prepare the OpenAPI 3.0.x Specification

MCP Server creation requires OpenAPI 3.0.0–3.0.3 (Swagger 2.0 is not supported — convert first).

Use the companion uas-reporting-oas3-sap-mcp-blog.json or adapt it to your own API. Key points in the spec:

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Resource Consumption
  version: "1.0"
  x-apiProvider: UAS_Reporting_Destination
  x-relativeUrl: /reports/v1

servers:
  - url: https://<integration-cell-virtual-host>/uas-reporting/v1

Resource paths in the spec should be relative to the Relative URL, not the full backend path. If x-relativeUrl is /reports/v1, the path for Cloud Credits is /cloudCreditsDetails — not /reports/v1/cloudCreditsDetails.

Step 3 — Create and Deploy the API Artifact

In Design → Integrations and APIs → Package → Artifacts → Add → API:

Field Value

RuntimeIntegration Cell
SourceURL or Specification (upload OpenAPI 3.0.3 file)
TargetDestination → UAS_Reporting_Destination
Relative URL/reports/v1
API Base Path/uas-reporting/v1
Virtual HostYour Integration Cell virtual host

Policies tab — Authorization:

Field Value

Authorization TypeOAuth Scope or Developer Key
ScopeAPI.invoke
Trust Upstream MCP Authorizationenabled

Then: Save → Deploy and confirm the artifact is started.

Validate the API before proceeding:

GET https://<virtual-host>/uas-reporting/v1/cloudCreditsDetails

Do not create the MCP Server until this returns 200.

Step 4 — Create and Deploy the MCP Server

Artifacts → Add → MCP Server, source type: API.

Field Value

APIResource Consumption
Name / IDResource_Consumption_mcpServer
MCP Path/uas-reporting
Version1.0.0
Runtime ProfileIntegration Cell
Virtual HostYour Integration Cell virtual host

In Create Tools, select the operations to expose. Review each generated Tool description — it is part of the contract the model uses to invoke that Tool.

Save → Deploy.

If the source API changes later (paths, parameters, auth), use Edit → Synchronize, then Save → Deploy the MCP Server. Without this, the MCP Server keeps stale tool definitions.

Step 5 — Validate the MCP Server

Run a complete smoke test before connecting Claude Code:

OAuth token → initialize → notifications/initialized → tools/list → tools/call

A tools/call that returns HTTP 200 with "isError": true means the transport worked but the Tool failed — check the Integration Suite processing logs for both the MCP Server and the API Artifact.

Useful first Tool call (Cloud Credits has no required date parameter):

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 3,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "<tool-name-from-tools-list>",
    "arguments": { "viewPhases": "CURRENT" }
  }
}

Step 6 — Publish in Developer Hub

Use the Developer Hub portal (not the design-time "Engage" capability). The correct path:

Admin Center → Content → Manage Content
→ Business Systems → open your system
→ MCP Servers tab → select your MCP Server
→ Create Product (Type: AI)
→ Publish

Publishing is asynchronous — track it in Admin Center → Scheduled Requests.

Once published, create an Agent Subscription:

Product → Subscribe → Create New Subscription for Agent

Leave the Callback URL empty. The subscription provides Token URL, Key (client ID), and Secret.

Step 7 — Add to Claude Code

claude mcp add \
  --transport http \
  --scope project \
  --client-id '<KEY>' \
  --client-secret \
  --callback-port 8080 \
  uas-reporting \
  'https://<integration-cell-virtual-host>/uas-reporting'

Enter the secret interactively. If it contains !, use:

read -s "SAP_MCP_CLIENT_SECRET?Client secret: "
export SAP_MCP_CLIENT_SECRET

Verify the connection with /mcp inside Claude Code.

Key Gotchas

Problem What to check

API missing from MCP source pickerMust be REST/OData, deployed on Integration Cell, OAuth-enabled, OpenAPI 3.0.x
Swagger 2.0 sourceConvert to OpenAPI 3.0.x first
Destination not visible to Integration CellIntegrationCell.Include=true must be under Labels, not Additional Properties
API Artifact 401 while backend worksInspect the MPL; verify the API runtime target is the Destination
403 with a valid tokenCheck authorization policy and token claims (auth ≠ authz)
Duplicate backend pathDestination URL + Relative URL + Resource Path must not repeat the prefix
API changed after MCP creationSynchronize → Save → Deploy
HTTP 200 with isError: trueTool execution failed; inspect MCP Server and API Artifact logs
Strange positional/named arguments in tools/callDo not use $ARGS as a jq variable — it is reserved
invalid authorization headerExtract token with jq -r '.access_token' to avoid whitespace
zsh: event not foundSecret contains !; enter interactively

 

References

  • SAP Help — Create an API Artifact Using a Target URL or an OpenAPI Specification
  • SAP Help — Create an MCP Server from an API Artifact
  • SAP Help — Synchronize API Changes to Your MCP Server
  • SAP Help — Developer Hub

entry.title: MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose S/4HANA Public Cloud API via OAuth2SAMLBearer
entry.content:
Introduction/Scenario

This post explains how to configure an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite to securely communicate with S/4HANA APIs using OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion. This approach ensures that API access is governed through individual user identities rather than a shared API user, providing better traceability and compliance.

For example, when a user interacts with an AI agent that is connected to the MCP server and accesses S/4HANA Public Cloud APIs, the user should only be able to view and manage data that they are authorized to access. This access is controlled by the user's assigned S/4HANA authorization and IAM roles, ensuring that existing security and governance policies are enforced.

Note: I encountered several issues while attempting to execute POST operations(create) against S/4HANA APIs through the MCP server. These challenges are described below. Any insights, recommendations, or similar experiences would be greatly appreciated.
Update: I have written a new article address some of the encountered issue via API-centric artifact - MCP Server with Integration Suite via API Centric ... - SAP Community

⚠️This is not a five-minute read. The article walks through every step, configuration, and consideration in detail, so give yourself enough time to absorb the information.

Flow:

→ Agent (Claude/Github Copilot/any AI Agent) 
  → MCP server by Integration Suite (Authenticated via IAS)
    → BTP Destination Service (OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion) 
        → S/4HANA Public Cloud (executed as the authenticated user)

Example testing through Github Copilot

Note:

  1. The Integration Suite API artifact is not used between the MCP server and S/4HANA because it does not currently support OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion. While a workaround is possible by retrieving the JWT token through a destination and overriding the generated API call with a custom Request-Reply step, this introduces additional complexity and requires considerable customization.
  2. This demonstration uses separate SAP Cloud Identity Services instances (with different client IDs) for different applications. However, depending on your security and governance requirements, you may choose to use a single Cloud Identity Services instance for multiple applications or user groups. For example, SAP BTP MCP could use the same client ID for all users accessing the solution through Single Sign-On (SSO).
  3. For S/4HANA Private Cloud scenarios, principal propagation should work as well by referring Principal Propagation from BTP Web App to S/4HANA via SAP Integration Suite.
  4. Previous example - User communicates with AI Agent (Sales Assistant) via Microsoft Copilot -> MCP server hosted in BTP via node.js -> S/4HANA Public Cloud API

Pre-requisite:

  • SAP BTP with Cloud Foundry Enabled
  • SAP Integration Suite with MCP server, Integration Cell runtime capability
  • S/4HANA Public Cloud 
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS)
  • AI Agent able to communicate with MCP server

Goto S/4HANA Public Cloud → Communication Arrangement App

Click on the "OAuth 2.0 Details"

Setup the MCP server in Integration Suite

Setting the MCP server quite similar to API, however it has limited API policy can be apply to the MCP server.
