entry.title: Connecting MCP Gateway on Integration Suite with Copilot Studio - Updating business partners
entry.content:
Over the last weeks I have been working on a tutorial series that shows how to connect Microsoft Copilot Studio with SAP through the MCP Gateway on SAP Integration Suite.

For an SAP-focused scenario, SAP Integration Suite is a very natural place to start. It already sits at the center of many enterprise integration landscapes, understands SAP APIs and connectivity patterns, and provides the governance, security, monitoring, and lifecycle capabilities that are needed when exposing business functionality beyond a single application.

This becomes especially important when AI agents enter the picture. Connecting an agent to SAP should not mean bypassing the integration layer or putting SAP credentials directly into the AI client. Instead, SAP Integration Suite can act as the controlled integration boundary: it exposes selected capabilities, handles connectivity to cloud or on-premise SAP systems, applies authentication and policy, and keeps operational responsibility where SAP teams already have the right tools.

The goal of the series is simple: start with a working MCP server, connect it to Copilot Studio, and then gradually move from a technical demo setup to a more realistic enterprise scenario with user authentication, SAP IAS, principal propagation, and finally read/write access to SAP business data.

The full tutorial series is available here:

https://github.com/hobru/sap-mcp-gateway-copilot-studio

Official SAP architecture reference

This setup is not just a personal experiment. The core principles are also documented in the official SAP Architecture Center reference architecture for Microsoft Copilot Studio and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite.

The reference architecture describes Copilot Studio as the MCP client and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite as the governed entry point for exposing SAP APIs, integration flows, and data sources as MCP-compliant tools.

You can find the official SAP Architecture Center page here:

Microsoft Copilot Studio and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite — SAP Architecture Center

The high-level architecture looks like this (see Microsoft Copilot Studio and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite | SAP Architecture Center )

 

This is also why I like SAP Integration Suite as the foundation for this scenario: it gives us the governed integration layer between AI agents and SAP systems. Authentication, routing, policies, monitoring, and backend connectivity stay in SAP BTP, while Copilot Studio provides the conversational front end.

Why this series?

MCP is becoming an important pattern for connecting AI agents and enterprise systems. SAP has also documented the MCP Gateway on SAP Integration Suite as one of the supported architectural options for exposing SAP capabilities to AI clients.

Connecting Copilot Studio to MCP Gateway raises a few questions:

  • How do we secure this properly?
  • How does user identity flow from Microsoft Entra ID to SAP?
  • Can we use SAP IAS as the SAP-native identity layer?
  • Can we reach an on-premise SAP backend through Cloud Connector?
  • Can the call run as the real ABAP user?
  • And finally: can we go beyond read-only scenarios and update SAP data safely?

That is what the tutorial series walks through step by step.

Tutorial series overview

 
Part Topic What it covers Video
1MCP Gateway on SAP Integration SuiteBuild the first MCP server and connect via Azure API Management using client credentialsWatch
2User authentication with Microsoft Entra IDUse OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow and connect directly from Copilot StudioWatch
3User authentication with SAP IASFederate Entra ID into SAP IAS and issue SAP-native tokensWatch
4On-prem principal propagationConnect to an on-prem SAP backend via Cloud Connector and execute as the real ABAP userWatch
5Bulk connector automationGenerate and deploy Copilot Studio connectors for all SAP MCP Gateway endpoints—
6ABAP MCP server via BTP RouterAlternative architecture using abap-ai/mcp2 inside ABAP, fronted by the BTP RouterWatch
7Updating SAP dataAdd a write scenario using an OData API artifact, stored backend credentials, and CSRF-token handlingWatch

 

The latest part: updating SAP data

The latest video in the series focuses on the missing piece in many demos: updating information in SAP, not just reading it.

 

In this part, the scenario returns to SAP Integration Suite MCP Gateway and adds an OData API artifact that calls API_BUSINESS_PARTNER.

The interesting part here is the split between:

  • the user-facing authentication from Copilot Studio into the MCP Gateway, using the previously established IAS setup, and
  • the backend authentication from Integration Suite into SAP, using a dedicated SAP communication user stored securely in Integration Suite security material.

This means the MCP client does not need to handle SAP credentials, cookies, or CSRF tokens directly. Integration Suite takes care of the backend communication, including the CSRF-token exchange required for PATCH operations.

The tutorial proves the flow by:

  1. Reading a Business Partner through the API.
  2. Updating selected information through a PATCH request.
  3. Reading the Business Partner again to confirm the change.
  4. Exposing the read and update operations as MCP tools for Copilot Studio.

Lessons learned

One important takeaway is that the identity and integration choices matter early.

For example, Parts 2 and 3 both give us a real user at the MCP Gateway level. But if the goal is to continue that identity into SAP through Cloud Connector and principal propagation, the SAP IAS-based setup from Part 3 becomes the more relevant foundation.

Another takeaway is that read scenarios and write scenarios have different requirements. Reading data through an MCP tool is already powerful, but updating SAP data requires more discipline around authorization, API scope, CSRF handling, backend credentials, and which operations should actually be exposed to an AI agent.

That is why the repository includes focused OpenAPI definitions and .http files with placeholders only, rather than exposing broad SAP APIs without review.

When to use which part

If you are new to the topic, I recommend starting with Part 1 and then following the sequence.

If you already have an MCP Gateway setup and mainly care about authentication, start with Part 2 or Part 3.

If your target is an on-premise SAP backend with real user context, Part 4 is the key one.

If you want to automate connector creation at scale, look at Part 5.

If you prefer running the MCP server inside ABAP, Part 6 shows a lighter alternative using the ABAP MCP SDK and the BTP Router.

And if you want to move from read-only scenarios to actual SAP updates, Part 7 is the one to watch.

Links

GitHub repository:
https://github.com/hobru/sap-mcp-gateway-copilot-studio

Official SAP Architecture Center reference:
https://architecture.learning.sap.com/docs/ref-arch/d2e34e

Videos:

  • Part 1: MCP Gateway on SAP Integration Suite
  • Part 2: User authentication with Microsoft Entra ID
  • Part 3: User authentication with SAP IAS
  • Part 4: On-prem principal propagation
  • Part 6: ABAP MCP server via BTP Router
  • Part 7: Updating SAP data through the MCP Gateway

Closing paragraph

I hope this series helps others who are looking at SAP Integration Suite, MCP Gateway, and Microsoft Copilot Studio together. The individual parts can be used independently, but together they show a path from a simple first connection all the way to authenticated, enterprise-ready SAP integration scenarios — including updating SAP data through the MCP Gateway.

entry.title: Retrieval of Application Runbooks from Private GitHub Repositories Using SAP Cloud Integration
entry.content:
In many enterprise environments, application source code and its supporting documentation are maintained in private GitHub repositories. Along with source code, these repositories often contain important Markdown files such as application documentation, architecture details, deployment instructions, troubleshooting guides, and operational runbooks.

In my Previous Blog , I covered how to integrate SAP Cloud Integration with a public GitHub repository using Open Connectors and retrieve file content. In this blog, I’m taking that approach further by working with a private GitHub repository and dynamically retrieving application documentation.

Use Case

While working on an integration project, we had a requirement to retrieve application-specific documentation whenever an integration error occurred.

During DEV  to QA and QA to UAT deployments, integrations were monitored for failures. When an error occurred, the exception handling flow would be triggered to retrieve the relevant runbook from the application's private GitHub repository. This documentation helped the development or support team understand the application and troubleshoot the issue.

The requirement was to dynamically identify the required document based on the repository owner, repository name, and file path, instead of manually searching for it in GitHub.

By the end of this blog, you’ll have a clear understanding of how to:

  1. Create a custom GitHub connector in SAP Open Connectors.
  2. Securely authenticate with a private GitHub repository using a Personal Access Token.
  3. Define reusable GitHub API resources in Open Connectors.
  4. Connect SAP Cloud Integration with the custom Open Connectors connector.
  5. Dynamically pass the repository owner, repository name, and file path from CPI.
  6. Retrieve application-specific runbooks content from GitHub.

Solution Overview

Step 1: Create a Personal Access Token in GitHub

Since we are working with a private GitHub repository, authentication is required to access the repository and its files through the GitHub API.

  1. Log in to GitHub and open Settings.
  2. Navigate to Developer settings -> Personal access tokens -> Fine-grained tokens.
  3. Click Generate new token.
  4. Provide a suitable name and select the required repository under Repository access.
  5. Under Repository permissions, provide read-only access to Contents.
  6. Generate the token and securely store it.

 

Step 2: Create a Custom Connector in SAP Open Connectors

According to requirement, we used a Custom Connector in SAP Open Connectors to have the flexibility to define the GitHub APIs and authentication required for dynamically retrieving application documentation.

We used SAP Open Connectors to simplify GitHub integration by centralizing authentication and securely managing the Personal Access Token. It also allowed us to define reusable GitHub API resources and connect them to SAP Cloud Integration, keeping the iFlow simple and flexible for dynamically retrieving files from private repositories.

Although SAP Open Connectors provides a standard GitHub connector, the custom connector allowed us to define the required resources according to our use case and pass the repository owner, repository name, and file path dynamically.

Fill in the required details and Once the details are entered, click Save & Next to continue with the connector configuration.

 

Step 3: Configure the Custom Connector

After clicking Save & Next, the Setup section is displayed. This section is used to configure the properties, authentication, configurations, parameters, and hooks required for the connector.

  1. Configure the Properties

Under Properties, enter the GitHub REST API base URL and configure the request and response headers.

           

            2. Configure the Personal Access Token

Under Configurations, add a configuration key for the GitHub Personal Access Token.

key - github.personal.access.token

The fine-grained Personal Access Token generated earlier is maintained using this configuration.This allows the token to be used by the connector without passing it directly from the SAP Cloud Integration flow.

           3.Configure the PreRequest Hook

The purpose of this hook is to add the GitHub Personal Access Token to the Authorization header before the request is sent to GitHub.

let vendorHeaders = request_vendor_headers;

vendorHeaders["Authorization"] =
    "Bearer " + configuration["github.personal.access.token"];

done({
    "request_vendor_headers": vendorHeaders
});

 

Step 4: Create the GitHub API Resources

After configuring the hook, navigate to the Resources tab. Here, we define the GitHub REST API endpoints required for our use case.

For our scenario, create the following resource

Select GET as the HTTP method.

Here, owner, repo, and path are configured as path parameters. These parameters allow us to dynamically identify the GitHub repository and the file to be retrieved.

After configuring the resource, click Save.

 

 

Step 5: Create and Authenticate the Connector Instance

After clicking Authenticate Instance, enter the GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) generated earlier in the configuration field and click Update to authenticate the connector instance.

As shown below, the GetFileContent API is now successfully authenticated and ready to be tested.

After entering the details in Tryout, click Execute to test the GetFileContent API and retrieve the requested file from the private GitHub repository.

After executing the API, we receive a 200 OK response, confirming that the request was successful. The response contains the details of the requested file, including its file type and Base64-encoded content, which can be further processed in SAP Cloud Integration.

 

Step 6: Storing Open Connectors Credentials in Security Material

Before using SAP Open Connectors in your iFlow, you need to store the required credentials in SAP Integration Suite.

 

Step 7: Connecting SAP Cloud Integration (CPI) to GitHub using Open Connectors

Once your GitHub instance is set up and running, the next step is to connect it with SAP Cloud Integration so you can retrieve file content from the repository.

To do this, start by creating a new iFlow in your CPI workspace. Add a Sender step, such as a Timer or HTTPS adapter, based on how you want to trigger the flow. Then, add a Receiver step.

For the Receiver, choose the Open Connectors adapter from the list of available adapters. This adapter will be used to connect CPI with GitHub through SAP Open Connectors.

  • The incoming request is in JSON format. We use the JSON to XML Converter to convert it into XML.This is required because we need to extract the individual values using XPath in the next step.
  • We use a Content Modifier to extract the owner, repo, and path values and store them as Exchange Properties.  

 Source Value: //*[local-name()='owner']/text()

Similarly, we create properties for repo and path.

  • The Request Reply is connected to the Open Connectors receiver, which uses the custom GitHub connector created earlier

  • The response received from GitHub is in JSON format. Therefore, we use another JSON to XML Converter to convert the response into XML.This allows us to easily access the content field using XPath.

  • At this stage, we use a Content Modifier to extract only the content field from the response.

  • This is important because we don't want to pass the complete GitHub JSON response to the decoder. We only need the Base64-encoded file content.

  •  

 

  • After extracting the content field, we use the Base64 Decoder to decode it and obtain the original file content.For example, if the file is a Markdown runbook, the decoded output contains the actual Markdown documentation.

After the flow executes successfully, all the steps are completed without errors, and the requested GitHub file content is retrieved.

 

The decoded content can be viewed in the Message Content section, where the original documentation from the GitHub repository is available for further processing or troubleshooting.

 

Conclusion

In this blog, we extended the GitHub integration approach from a public repository to a private GitHub repository using a custom connector in SAP Open Connectors. By defining the required GitHub API resource and handling authentication through a Personal Access Token, we can securely access application-specific documentation.

The Cloud Integration iFlow further makes the solution reusable by dynamically accepting the repository owner, repository name, and file path at runtime. When an integration error occurs, the relevant runbook can therefore be retrieved from the application's repository and processed for troubleshooting, helping development and support teams access the required documentation without manually searching through GitHub.

This approach demonstrates how SAP Cloud Integration, Open Connectors, and GitHub can be combined to provide a flexible and reusable process for retrieving application documentation as part of an integration support process.

If you have any questions or would like a downloadable iFlow sample, feel free to drop a comment.

entry.title: Expose RFCs as MCP Tools in Integration Suite
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP systems hold decades of business logic. The RFC function modules that drive procurement, order management, inventory, and finance have been refined over years of production use. Until recently, that logic was accessible only to other SAP systems or middleware that understood the RFC protocol. An AI agent had no path to it.

The RFC as MCP capability in SAP Integration Suite changes this. We can expose SAP RFC function modules as MCP tools, which makes the business logic available to AI agents through a standardised protocol.

This blog walks through how to configure an RFC-based MCP server on Integration Suite and illustrates the outcome with a real procurement scenario.

In short: Bring any RFC → turn it into a ready-to-use agent tool.

Scenario: Creating a Purchase Order for Industrial Components

A procurement specialist needs to raise a purchase order for a batch of industrial components from a vendor. They open their AI assistant and provide the order details directly:

I need to create a purchase order with the following data:

Company Code0001
Document TypeNB
Vendor0001000141
Purchasing Organization0001
Purchasing Group100
Document Date20210303
CurrencyEUR
PO Item00010
Material6237-100-WL
Plant0001
Quantity30
Unit of Measure EA
Net Price30.00
Price Unit1
Delivery Date20210303


With an RFC-based MCP server running on SAP Integration Suite, the assistant calls a tool backed by BAPI_PO_CREATE1, a standard ABAP function module and creates the document directly in the ERP system.

Purchase Order 4500734787 created successfully.

The specialist then asks:

Show me the details of PO 4500734787.

The assistant calls a tool backed by BAPI_PO_GETDETAIL1, which returns the complete purchase order in a single call. The specialist confirms the header data, line item, and schedule line are exactly as specified.


Modelling the MCP Server

Navigate to your package under Design → Integrations and APIs → Artifacts, click Add, and select MCP Server.

Step 1: Select the Source Type

The first step in the wizard asks to choose the source from which the MCP server will be built. Integration Suite currently supports three source types:

  • API: Create an MCP server from an existing API artifact deployed on the Integration Cell.
  • HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification: Import an OpenAPI specification and expose operations from any HTTP endpoint.
  • RFC: Connect to an SAP backend via RFC and expose selected function modules as MCP tools.

Select RFC.

Select Source Step

Step 2: Select an RFC Destination

The wizard displays a list of RFC-capable destinations registered in the BTP subaccount. Select the destination that points to the SAP backend system containing the function modules you want to expose.

Before this step, confirm that the destination meets two prerequisites:

  1. The destination type is RFC with Proxy Type: On Premise.
  2. The destination has the label IntegrationCell.Include = true in its configuration. This label makes the destination discoverable within the MCP server creation wizard.

Select Destination Step

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Step 3: Search and select RFC Function Modules

With the destination selected, the wizard presents a search interface for RFC function modules on the connected backend.

  1. Enter a search term. The search requires a minimum of 7 characters. For e.g; BAPI_PO
  2. A list of matching function modules appears with names and descriptions pulled directly from the backend system.
  3. Select the function modules you want to expose as MCP tools. Each selected function module becomes one tool in the MCP server.
  4. Click Next.

Select Tools Step

Note:  A maximum of 50 tools can be added to the MCP server as of today.

Step 4: Provide the MCP Server Details

Provide MCP Details Step

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Configure and deploy MCP Server

Once the MCP Server has been created, you can further configure and customise it from the MCP Configuration tab before deploying it. The configuration is organised into three sections: Source, Tools and Prompts.

Note: The Resources section is not applicable for this source.

Source

The Source tab shows the RFC destination pointing to the ABAP system whose function modules were used to create the MCP Server.

Source Tab

Tools

The Tools tab lists all MCP tools exposed by the server. Each tool represents a business capability backed by an RFC function module in the ABAP system. New tools can also be added to the MCP server from this tab.

Selecting a tool reveals the following details:

  • RFC Function Name: The name of the underlying function module.
  • Tool Name: The identifier used in the MCP server. This field is editable and is what AI clients see when discovering available tools.
  • Title and Description: Editable fields that describe the business capability the tool exposes.
  • Input Schema: The parameters the AI application must provide when invoking the tool, derived from the function module's import, changing and table interfaces.
  • Output Schema: The structure of the response returned after the tool is executed, derived from the function module's export, changing and table interfaces.

AI agents rely on the tool name, title, and description to determine which tool is relevant for a given task. It is recommended that these fields clearly describe the business purpose of the tool in plain language.

Tools Schema View

Prompts

The Prompts tab allows you to define reusable prompt templates for the MCP Server. These templates guide AI applications on how to interact with the exposed tools for common business operations, reducing the need for users to construct detailed instructions from scratch each time.

Policies

A well-designed MCP Server exposes the right capabilities to AI agents and ensures those capabilities are accessed securely. Every MCP Server created in SAP Integration Suite is provisioned with a default policy model that can be customised to meet your organisation's security and governance requirements.

For an RFC-based MCP Server, two aspects differ from one created from an API source. The receiver adapter used at runtime is RFC rather than HTTP.  Additionally in order to invoke the MCP Server endpoint, the calling application must be authorised with the scopes API.invoke and ESBMessaging.send.

All other components and configurations in the Policy Modeler will remain the same as defined for creation of MCP Server from APIs implementation.

RFC receiver adapter

Scopes to invoke the MCP server

Once all the necessary configurations are completed, deploy the MCP Server. This makes the MCP Server endpoint available for invocation by AI agents.

Invoke the MCP Server Using Joule Desktop

I'll be using Joule Desktop to demonstrate the end-to-end flow. Joule Desktop is connected to the deployed MCP server using the credentials of a Process Integration Runtime (PIR) service instance. In order to understand the process to generate PIR credentials, please refer the blog from my colleague. 

As seen below, Joule Desktop is able to discover the tools successfully configured in the MCP server after a successful connection. These tools will now be used to create a purchase order and view it's details, based on the scenario described in the beginning of the blog.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Joule Desktop analyses the request and chooses the tool BAPI_PO_CREATE1 to create a purchase order in the ERP system.

Now that the PO has been successfully created, the next step is to retrieve its details. Joule Desktop invokes the BAPI_PO_GETDETAIL1 tool to fetch the relevant PO information, making it easy to access and review the details of the newly created purchase order.

Conclusion

To summarise, we have seen how an MCP Server can be created in SAP Integration Suite using RFC function modules as its source.

Previously, working with RFCs meant opening the relevant SAP transaction and manually performing each business operation. With this capability, the same operations can be performed by any MCP-compatible AI application, through a standardised protocol, without direct system access.

What makes this approach sustainable in an enterprise context is not just the connectivity. It is the governance layer that comes with it. Every MCP Server created in Integration Suite carries a policy model, enforces authorisation scopes, and participates in the same lifecycle management as any other integration asset.

Thanks for reading and I hope it helped to understand the concept of creating MCP Servers using RFC as the source. Please feel free to leave a comment and I would be happy to receive any feedback.

entry.title: SAP API Management: From Policy-Centric Proxies to API-Centric Integration
entry.content:
Update 28/09/2026 - Dynamic Routing on Integration Cell: Possible, but with an Important Constraint

A hands-on comparison between Classic API Management and the new Integration Cell runtime

SAP Integration Suite has historically kept two concerns relatively distinct: API Management for exposing, securing, governing, and controlling APIs, and Cloud Integration for routing, transformation, orchestration, and backend connectivity.

With API-Centric Integration and the Integration Cell runtime, that boundary becomes much smaller.

Instead of treating an API mainly as a proxy surrounded by policies, SAP now allows an API Artifact to contain API management capabilities together with integration logic and backend connectivity. Security, traffic management, routing, transformation, and connectivity can be modeled much closer together. SAP Help Portal

This article is not another introduction to API-Centric Integration. SAP already provides good material for that.

Instead, I wanted to answer a much more practical question:

What actually became simpler for someone who has been implementing APIs with Classic SAP API Management?

I implemented the same types of scenarios using both approaches and compared them side by side.

What is Integration Cell?

Integration Cell is SAP's managed, cloud-native runtime for running API Artifacts. SAP describes it as a Kubernetes-based runtime supporting API-centric integration, API composition, API simplification, security, traffic management, and API lifecycle governance. SAP Help Portal

The important change for an integration developer is not Kubernetes itself.

It is the development model.

With Classic API Management, an implementation can quickly become a collection of:

API Proxy
   ↓
Policies
   ↓
Target Endpoint
   ↓
  KVM
   ↓
JavaScript Routing DDCR
   ↓
Fault Rules
   ↓
Target Endpoint

With the Integration Cell runtime, the API Artifact can directly include integration capabilities:

API Artifact
   ↓
Security / Policies
   ↓
Integration Logic
   ↓
Routing / Transformation
   ↓
Backend Connectivity

SAP explicitly describes API-Centric Integration as allowing security, traffic management, and integration capabilities to coexist within a single development model. SAP Help Portal

The requirement did not disappear.

The implementation model changed.

From Policy-Centric to Integration-Centric

Classic API Management remains a supported runtime. Existing API proxies do not suddenly become obsolete because Integration Cell exists.

But the architectural difference is significant.

In the classic model, relatively simple requirements can involve several independent artifacts or policies. In the new model, many of those capabilities are directly represented inside the API Artifact and its integration model.

That becomes very visible with two simple examples:

CORS and Basic Authentication.

And this is where the comparison becomes more interesting than the product announcement itself.

Example 1 — CORS

In one of my existing Classic API Management implementations, CORS required an explicit policy that generated the required HTTP response headers.

For example:

<Set>
    <Headers>
        <Header name="Access-Control-Allow-Origin">*</Header>
        <Header name="Access-Control-Allow-Methods">
            GET, POST, OPTIONS
        </Header>
        <Header name="Access-Control-Allow-Headers">
            Content-Type, Authorization
        </Header>
    </Headers>
</Set>

Together with the position of that policy inside the API Proxy flow.

With the API Artifact running on Integration Cell, CORS is directly represented as configuration:

CORS
 ├─ Enabled
 ├─ Allowed Origins
 ├─ Allowed Headers
 ├─ Expose Headers
 ├─ Allowed Methods
 ├─ Max Age
 └─ Allow Credentials

Same requirement.

Considerably less implementation machinery.

Example 2 — Authentication and Backend Access

The same difference becomes even clearer with authentication.

In my Classic API Management implementation, the target-side flow used multiple elements:

KVM
 ↓
Basic Authentication Policy
 ↓
Raise Fault
 ↓
Target

The KVM stored configuration, JavaScript performed supporting logic, and fault handling had to be explicitly modeled.

With the new API Artifact, the equivalent flow can be modeled much closer to the integration itself:

Client
  ↓
Authentication
  ↓
Request Reply
  ↓
HTTP
  ↓
Target

And authentication becomes an explicit part of the model.

Dummy Demo for SAP SCN

To validate the new API-Centric Integration model, I created a very small end-to-end scenario using two SAP Integration Suite trial tenants.

In the first tenant, I created a basic API using API Management with the Integration Cell runtime. The API exposes a simple HTTPS endpoint and forwards the request to a backend system.

For the backend simulation, I used a second Cloud Integration trial tenant. There, I created a minimal integration flow containing only a Content Modifier, which returns the following response together with a timestamp:

API

url: https://cf3a5f71trial-fcda0e60d288400d91513ec5f99afd98.a.integration.cloud.sap/sales

 

Target endpoint:

Another CI Trial simulating the back end

Response:

UPDATE 28/09/2026 — Dynamic Routing on Integration Cell: Possible, but with an Important Constraint

After the initial point-to-point test, I wanted to validate a more important architectural scenario.

The question was simple:

Can one API Artifact expose a stable domain facade while dynamically routing requests to different backend systems ?

This is important because a domain-oriented API should not require a new artifact every time the physical backend, region, or implementation changes.

The target architecture was:

Consumer
   ↓
Stable Domain Facade
   ↓
Routing Metadata
   ↓
Metadata Resolution
   ↓
Router
   ↓
Physical Backend

For the test, the API facade remained:

POST /sales

Behind that facade, I configured multiple possible routes.

For example:

SAP ECC
S/4HANA US
Another target

The Policy Model contained:

Authentication
      ↓
Content Modifier
      ↓
Control Plane - Content Modifier
      ↓
Groovy
      ↓
Router
   ├── Route 1
   ├── Route 2
   └── Route 3

The dynamic routing itself worked.

The limitation appeared in how the routing context reached the Policy Model.

Control Plane:

Groovy:

The old  import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message does not works into Policy

Only with new import

import com.sap.it.script.v2.api.Message

def Message processData(Message message) {

    String path = message.getHeader("path", String.class)
    String mappings = message.getBody(String.class)

    if (!path) {
        throw new Exception("CamelHttpPath not found")
    }

    // Normalize incoming path without regex
    path = path.trim()

    while (path.startsWith("/")) {
        path = path.substring(1)
    }

    if (path.startsWith("sales/")) {
        path = path.substring(6)
    }

    String targetUrl = null

    int start = 0
    int length = mappings.length()

    // Single-pass scan: no split(), no arrays, no closures
    while (start < length) {

        int end = mappings.indexOf(';', start)

        if (end < 0) {
            end = length
        }

        int comma = mappings.indexOf(',', start)

        if (comma > start && comma < end) {

            int keyStart = start

            // Skip leading whitespace
            while (keyStart < comma &&
                   Character.isWhitespace(mappings.charAt(keyStart))) {
                keyStart++
            }

            // Skip leading slash(es)
            while (keyStart < comma &&
                   mappings.charAt(keyStart) == '/') {
                keyStart++
            }

            // Skip optional sales/ prefix
            if ((comma - keyStart) >= 6 &&
                mappings.regionMatches(keyStart, "sales/", 0, 6)) {
                keyStart += 6
            }

            int keyEnd = comma

            // Remove trailing whitespace
            while (keyEnd > keyStart &&
                   Character.isWhitespace(mappings.charAt(keyEnd - 1))) {
                keyEnd--
            }

            int keyLength = keyEnd - keyStart

            // Compare without creating a temporary key String
            if (keyLength == path.length() &&
                mappings.regionMatches(keyStart, path, 0, keyLength)) {

                int urlStart = comma + 1
                int urlEnd = end

                while (urlStart < urlEnd &&
                       Character.isWhitespace(mappings.charAt(urlStart))) {
                    urlStart++
                }

                while (urlEnd > urlStart &&
                       Character.isWhitespace(mappings.charAt(urlEnd - 1))) {
                    urlEnd--
                }

                targetUrl = mappings
                    .substring(urlStart, urlEnd)
                    .replace("\\://", "://")

                // First exact match wins
                break
            }
        }

        start = end + 1
    }

    if (!targetUrl) {
        throw new Exception("Route not found for: " + path)
    }

    message.setProperty("targetUrl", targetUrl)

    return message
}

HTTPS:

Custom Routing                                                                                                                    Fix Value API HTTP Channel.

 

 

 

 

The request path could not be used as expected

My original intention was to expose paths such as:

/sales/orders/create/sapecc

and:

/sales/orders/create/s4hana/us

and use the additional path segments directly as routing metadata.

In my current Integration Cell implementation, this did not work as expected.

The API endpoint effectively had to remain fixed:

/sales

The working alternative was to provide the additional routing information using a custom HTTP header.

For example:

POST /sales
path: /orders/create/sapecc

and:

POST /sales
path: /orders/create/s4hana/us

The Policy Model could then read that value, process it, and route the request correctly.

Both backend routes were successfully executed through the same API facade.

Why this matters architecturally

This is not simply a technical inconvenience.

It affects how teams may naturally design APIs on Integration Cell.

The simplest implementation model today can easily become:

/sales-ecc
      ↓
API Artifact
      ↓
SAP ECC
 
/sales-s4-us
      ↓
API Artifact
      ↓
S/4HANA US
 
/sales-s4-eu
      ↓
API Artifact
      ↓
S/4HANA EU

Technically, each integration works.

Architecturally, however, the landscape starts accumulating artifacts whose primary difference is only the physical destination.

That brings us back to a problem I have been discussing throughout this year:

integration artifact proliferation - API SPRAWL.

The issue is not that Integration Cell cannot perform dynamic routing.

It can.

The issue is that without a deliberate metadata-resolution layer, the most straightforward implementation model encourages relatively static API-to-backend relationships.

At scale, this can produce:

duplicated API Artifacts
duplicated routing logic
duplicated security configuration
duplicated error handling
duplicated backend configuration

The technical implementation becomes simpler locally, but the overall landscape can become more complex globally.

DDCR (Domain Driven-Centric Router) with Control Plane - Content Modifier

I extended the POC to validate whether the Integration Cell API Artifact could support the same DDCR — Domain-Driven Centric Router principle I previously implemented with Classic API Management.

The objective was simple:

Stable Facade
     ↓
Routing Metadata
     ↓
Control Plane - Content Modifier
     ↓
Router
     ↓
SAP ECC / S/4HANA

The API facade remained fixed:

POST /sales

As routing metadata.

The working approach was to keep /sales stable and provide the routing information through a custom header:

 
path: /orders/create/sapecc
path: /orders/create/s4hana/us

For this POC, the Control Plane was intentionally simple: a Content Modifier containing the routing metadata:

/sales/orders/create/sapecc,<SAP ECC URL>;
/sales/orders/create/s4hana/us,<S/4HANA URL>;

A Groovy Script compared the incoming path header with this metadata and resolved the destination. The result was then evaluated by a Router.

Authentication
     ↓
Control Plane
     ↓
Groovy Resolution
     ↓
Router
   ↙       ↘
SAP ECC   S/4HANA

The same /sales API Artifact successfully routed requests to two different backend simulations.

This proves that dynamic routing is possible on Integration Cell, but it also exposed an important limitation: without an explicit routing mechanism, the current model naturally favors static API-to-backend relationships, which can lead to unnecessary API Artifact proliferation.

The custom path header was used only to validate the routing concept. In a mature DDCR implementation, consumer-facing metadata should represent business intent rather than expose physical backend names.

I have already covered the same architectural principle from other integration perspectives. The following articles and The Integration Cut episodes provide additional context, the new blog for API Integration Cell will use the same architecture decision as I did below:

SAP BTP - CI - Immutable Event Routing per Domain with Metadata-Driven Consumer Orchestration

Again, the security requirement did not disappear.

My Current Assessment

API-Centric Integration clearly reduces much of the policy glue found in Classic API Management. CORS, authentication, routing, and backend connectivity can now live inside the same API Artifact.

However, my hands-on test exposed two limitations:

  • Dynamic target resolution is limited. The target URL remains fixed, so more advanced routing required custom metadata, Groovy, and a Router. Without that extra abstraction, the model can easily drift toward point-to-point API proliferation.
  • Complex routing can become hard to maintain. In my test, additional independent End Message elements were not available, so multiple branches must converge again, which can quickly turn the Policy Model into a spider web.

The technology makes individual integrations easier to build.

Governance determines whether the landscape remains simple at scale.

What disappeared was much of the policy glue around it.

  • SAP Help — API Management SAP Help Portal
  • SAP Help — API Artifact / API Lifecycle SAP Help Portal
  • SAP Help — Get Started with Integration Cell SAP Help Portal
  • SAP Help — Design APIs and MCP Servers / Supported Runtimes SAP Help Portal
  • SAP Community — API-Centric Integration on SAP Integration Suite – Part 1 SAP Community

Kind regards,

Viana.

entry.title: MCP Server with Integration Suite via API Centric Integration, S/4HANA API
entry.content:
Introduction/Scenario

This post continues from the previous article, MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose S/4HANA ... - SAP Community, and focuses on addressing the identified issues by using API Artifacts.
 
Important Update 2026-Oct-02: The workaround on handling the SSO Authentication no longer valid as SAP updates not allowing developer to remove the auto generated HTTP channel in API artifact anymore. Of course, there is other workaround which considered dirty tick that I would not keen to share this publicly. Let wait for the official released by SAP on supporting the principal propagation. 
However, the handling of CSRF token or etag approach still valid.

Background:

The previous post demonstrated how to set up an MCP server with SAP Integration Suite and connect it to S/4HANA Public Cloud using OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion. This approach helps maintain governance by ensuring that S/4HANA APIs are consumed using a named user account, where access is restricted based on the authorizations and roles assigned to that user.

When the MCP server is used for read-only scenarios, such as HTTP GET operations, it works well with clients such as GitHub Copilot and Claude. However, several issues were encountered when attempting to perform write operations against S/4HANA Public Cloud APIs, such as HTTP POST (create) and PATCH (update) requests through the MCP server.

Therefore, the approach described in this post is optional and only relevant if your MCP server needs to support create or update operations on S/4HANA APIs. If your use case is limited to HTTP GET requests, you can continue to follow the implementation approach described in the previous blog without the additional steps covered here.

Note: SAP may enhance Integration Suite in future releases to support these scenarios out of the box. As a result, the workaround described in this post may eventually become obsolete. Before implementing this approach, always refer to the latest SAP documentation available on SAP Help Portal to verify whether a native solution is available.

 

Issue CountIssue Detail
1

Data type that interpreted as object as example below, where causing issue when calling the MCP server.

Thanks @MioYasutake, shared the workaround to remove the "anyOf" in the OpenAPI specification with a plain type, that shall resolve this issue if direct expose the S/4HANA API via the MCP server.

However, the approach shared in this blog does not need touch the OpenAPI specification.

2

 Getting error as it is trying to convert the content before perform API call

Current workaround: Remove all the SAP_Messages and SAP__Messages from the downloaded OpenAPI file and load into the integration suite MCP server again. But this is touching the OpenAPI file that downloaded from api.sap.com. Looks like there is no other option beside touching the specification file.

 

3

CSRF token issue when doing HTTP Post action, looks like there is no way to enhance the MCP to send access HTTP header and update the MCP server to handle this.

This blog is demonstrating the possible option to resolve this.

4

ETag handling when doing HTTP patch action

This blog is demonstrating the possible option to resolve this.

5

Other data type issues, for example "Time" don't seem working as expected in Postman, SAP return "HH:MM:SS", but "Time" data type is expecting "HH:MM:SS{Z}" instead if not mistaken. Will need to remove the "Time Format" in the API artifact or update the OpenAPI specification prior loaded into the API artifact. 

The response in the Postman console

 The MCP artifact/policies only allows limited API policies application (refer - Configure an MCP Server Created from an API Artifact | SAP Help Portal), and no message transformation or additional HTTP called is allowed. Hence, this writing is demonstrating how to use the API Centric Artifact on solving some of the mentioned issued below and still supporting user principal propagation connection to the S/4HANA Public Cloud API.

Note:

  1. As of the date of writing, the API-centric artifacts and policies in SAP Integration Suite do not support principal propagation. During Devtoberfest 2026 From APIs to Agent Tools: How MCP Gateway changes what Integration means - YouTube, SAP indicated that this capability is on the roadmap for a future release. Therefore, this blog demonstrates a possible workaround to achieve principal propagation until native support becomes available.
  2. In addition, the final section of this blog shows how principal propagation can be implemented when connecting to SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud or SAP S/4HANA On-Premise via SAP Cloud Connector.

→ Agent (Claude/Github Copilot/any AI Agent) 
  → MCP server by Integration Suite (Authenticated via IAS)
    → API Artifact by Integration Suite (Authenticated via IAS)
        → BTP Destination Service (OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion)

  • Will leverage the BTP destination API to generate SAML bearer assertion token to access the S/4HANA public cloud to overcome the limitation that API artifact don't support OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion. Reference

  • SAP Integration Suite with MCP server, Integration Cell runtime capability
  • S/4HANA Public Cloud 
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS)
  • AI Agent able to communicate with MCP server
  • The BTP destination to S/4HANA Public Cloud already setup - refer previous blog

  • Plan: lite
  • Create a key and copy the Client ID, Client Secret and uri for later usage

Create API Artifact

Important: Remove all the SAP_Messages and SAP__Messages from the downloaded OpenAPI file. You may use AI assistant on helping this if not familiar on changing this. 

Create a new API Artifact - choose Integration Cell as the Runtime Profile

Select URL or  Specification

Enter the information as below

  • URL: URL to access the S/4HANA public cloud sales order api
  • Name: your prefer name
  • ID: your prefer ID
  • Service Type: REST
  • API Base Path: your prefer path

Update description if required

The URL here will be come irrelevant to the policies as will overwrite the auto generated endpoint

Resources are auto generated based on the uploaded API specification

Policies

Important here: delete the auto generated target HTTP channel, recreate a new HTTP channel to target or S/4HANA Public Cloud API, as the default generated target HTTP channel not allowing the "Authorization" header passing

More information can refer to the blog Secure APIs: External OIDC-Based Authentication fo... - SAP Community

  • The Well-known URL: https://<ias tenant>.accounts.ondemand.com/.well-known/openid-configuration
  • Audience: Can leave empty unless restrict to certain client ID or target system only
  • ClientID Key: standard using ${authn.oidc.jwt.azp}, where you can find out this when studying the JWT via any JWT decoder, for example: SuperTokens JWT Decoder
  • User Info Key: standard using ${authn.oidc.jwt.email}, where you can find out this when studying the JWT via any JWT decoder, for example: SuperTokens JWT Decoder

 

import com.sap.it.script.v2.api.Message;
import groovy.json.JsonOutput;
import groovy.json.JsonSlurper;

def Message storeInputInformation(Message message) {
    
    Map<String, Object> headers = message.getHeaders();
    
    // Convert to JSON string
    String headersJson = JsonOutput.prettyPrint(JsonOutput.toJson(headers))
    // Store in exchange property
    message.setProperty("OriHeaders", headersJson);
    
    message.setProperty("OriBody", message.getBody());
    
    // get token
    String authHeader = message.getHeader("Authorization", String)
    String token = authHeader?.replaceFirst(/^Bearer\s+/, "")
    message.setProperty("AccessToken", token)
    
    // set token for destination fetch
    message.setHeader("x-user-token", token)
    
    return message;
}

 

Request-Reply to Destination Service

  • Address: <uri copy from the destination service instance key>/v1/destinations/<destination created in BTP>, for example: https://destination-configuration.cfapps.us10.hana.ondemand.com/destination-configuration/v1/destinations/S4_XBB_API
  • Credential Name: The credential artifact the capture the OAuth2ClientCredential setup, this token URL, client ID and password refer to the Destination Service Instance key
  • Request Headers: x-user-token

 

 

Extract Token return from destination, where this Token can be used to call S/4HANA

def Message extractTokenFromDestination(Message message) {
    
    // set back original headers
    String headersJson = message.getProperty("OriHeaders")
    if (headersJson) {
        def headersMap = new JsonSlurper().parseText(headersJson)
        headersMap.each { key, value ->
            if (value != null) {
                message.setHeader(key.toString(), value.toString())
            }
        }
    }

    def json = new JsonSlurper().parseText(message.getBody(String))

    def bearerToken = json.authTokens?.find { it.type == "Bearer" }?.value
    message.setHeader("Authorization", "Bearer ${bearerToken}")
    message.setProperty("SAMLBearerAssertionToken", bearerToken);
    
    message.setBody(message.getProperty("OriBody"));

    return message;
}

 

Router to decide fetch CSRF token

 

Content Modifier: Set CSRF Token Fetch Header

 

Request Reply - Fetch CSRF Token

  • Address: <api URL>
  • Proxy Type: Internet
  • Method: GET
  • Authentication: none (token already set in previous step, will be pass at request header)
  • Request Headers: Authorization|x-csrf-token
  • Response Headers: *

 

Extract CSRF response cookie and set cookie

def Message extractCSRFToken(Message message) {
    
    def cookies = message.getHeader("set-cookie");
    message.setHeader("cookie", String.join("; ", cookies));
    
    return message;
}

 

Router - set Etag header, set to * always also force update

 

 Set the original input header and body before perform the HTTP call to the actual target API URL

def Message prepareInputPriorCall(Message message) {
    // keep a copy of the cookies as this is returned by the CSRF token fetch
    def cookies = message.getHeader("cookie");
    
    // set back original headers
    String headersJson = message.getProperty("OriHeaders")
    if (headersJson) {
        def headersMap = new JsonSlurper().parseText(headersJson)
        headersMap.each { key, value ->
            if (value != null) {
                message.setHeader(key.toString(), value.toString())
            }
        }
    }
    
    // pass the bearer token as authorization header
    def bearerToken = message.getProperty("SAMLBearerAssertionToken");
    message.setHeader("Authorization", "Bearer ${bearerToken}")
    
    message.setBody(message.getProperty("OriBody"));
    
    // set back the CSRF token fetch cookie
    message.setHeader("cookie", cookies);
    
    return message;
}

 

Actual Request-Reply to the API URL based on the input

  • Address: <api URL>${header.camelhttppath}
  • Query: ${header.camelhttpquery}
  • Proxy Type: Internet
  • Method: Dynamic
  • Expression: ${header.camelhttpmethod}
  • Send Body: checkbox ticked
  • Authentication: none (token already set in previous step, will be pass at request header)
  • Request Headers: *
  • Response Headers: *

entry.title: Building an MCP Server on Integration Cell, part of SAP Integration Suite : APIs to AI Agents
entry.content:
Credit : In a series of super blogs, my colleague @Ashutosh_KSingh has explained how to set up Integration Cell, What is API Centric Integration and How to get started with MCP servers on Integration Suite. 

https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-sap/api-centric-integration-on-sap-integration-suite-part-1-build-and-deploy/ba-p/14438357

https://community.sap.com/t5/integration-blog-posts/mcp-servers-on-sap-integration-suite-build-your-first-mcp-server-from-an/ba-p/14441034

This Blog post builds on this knowledge and works on a scenario comparing SuccessFactors API Consumption via Application vs Agents, powered by MCP servers on Integration Cell.

 

A New Way to Deliver HR Self-Service

It is 9 AM on a Monday. John Smith has just joined ABC Corp and is sitting through onboarding. The HR presenter mentions the Company Car benefit.

John wants to know what cars he can choose, which vendors are approved, what the lease rates look like, and whether he is already enrolled. The presenter points him to the employee portal.

John opens the portal. It does exactly what it was built to do — he finds a Car Options screen with approved models, vendors, and lease providers, and a second screen showing his enrollment status. The portal works well for the questions it was designed to answer.

Then John asks a follow-up: "Which provider gives me the best deal for a Toyota?" That one is not on any screen. He opens a helpdesk ticket and gets a reply two days later.

This is a familiar and reasonable situation. HR portals are purpose-built, well-governed, and take significant effort to deliver — typically 8 to 12 weeks. They serve the majority of employee needs well. The challenge is the long tail: every new question that was not anticipated at design time either goes unanswered or triggers a new development sprint.

This blog introduces a complementary approach — using Integration Cell, part of SAP Integration Suite's MCP capability to expose the same SuccessFactors APIs as AI agent tools, so that employees can ask questions in natural language and get answers beyond what any fixed screen provides.


Part 1: The Data Model — SuccessFactors Company Car APIs

Before building anything, it helps to understand what APIs we are working with.

SAP SuccessFactors exposes its benefits domain via OData v2. The Company Car benefit has six entities, arranged in three clean layers.

The Three Layers

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Layer 1 — Reference Data                               │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐     │
│  │ AllowedModels        │  │ RecommendedVendors   │     │
│  │ Toyota, Nissan, VW   │  │ Hertz, AVIS          │     │
│  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐                │
│  │ LeaseServiceProvider                │                │
│  │ AVIS Rental (10.20%), LeasePlan     │                │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────┘                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 2 — Policy                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ BenefitCompanyCar                                │   │
│  │ Lock-in period, maintenance, buyback, EMI freq   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Layer 3 — Employee Transactions                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐     │
│  │ CompanyCarEnrollment  │  │ CompanyCarClaim     │     │
│  │ John's enrollment     │  │ John's claims       │     │
│  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The full API spec is available on SAP API Business Accelerator Hub: https://hub.sap.com/api/ECGlobalBenefits/overview

Part 2: Building the MCP Server on SAP Integration Suite

SAP Integration Suite's Integration Cell runtime supports creating MCP servers directly from an OpenAPI specification — no custom code required. Here is how to set it up, step by step.

Step 1 — Get the OpenAPI Spec

Download the API spec from SAP API Business Accelerator Hub (search for "Global Benefits"). The spec is in OpenAPI 2.0 (Swagger) format.

Important: Integration Suite's MCP server requires OpenAPI 3.0. Use any AI tool (or the Swagger Converter) to upgrade the spec from 2.0 to 3.0 before proceeding.

Step 2 — Create an Integration Package

Log in to your Integration Suite tenant and navigate to Design → Integration Packages. Create a new integration package to hold your MCP server artifact.

Step 3 — Add an MCP Server Artifact

Inside the package, click Add → MCP Server.

In the creation wizard:

  • Select HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification as the connection type
  • Set Method to Upload
  • Upload your OpenAPI 3.0 spec file
  • Set the virtual host path — for example: <Virtual Host>/sfsf

 

This is where your MCP endpoint URL will be hosted.

Step 4 — Select Your Tools

After uploading the spec, the wizard discovers all available API paths as potential tools. Search for "Company Car" in the search field and select all 12 related tools. Click Add.

 The MCP server artifact is now created.

Step 5 — Configure Tools, Prompts, and Resources

Open the MCP server artifact and switch to the MCP Configuration tab. You will see four sections: Source | Tools | Resources | Prompts.

 


Under Tools, you can:

  • View all selected tools
  • Add or remove tools
  • Click any tool to inspect its Input Schema and Output Schema
  • Edit tool names and descriptions in edit mode

Pro tip: Invest time in editing tool descriptions. The natural language description you write for each tool is what the AI agent reads when deciding which tools to call. A clear description like "Returns the list of car models the company has approved for the benefit program" is far more useful to an agent than "BenefitCompanyCarAllowedModels".

Similarly, the Prompts and Resources sections can be enriched with additional context per the MCP specification.

Step 6 — Configure Policies

Click the Policies section to view what is applied to the MCP endpoint.

 

Authentication and Authorization are applied by default.

In the Authentication policy settings, add Basic authentication — this supports Process Integration Runtime (PIR) credentials, which is how agents will authenticate when calling the MCP server. OAuth (client credentials) and Client Certificate authentication are also supported.

 

For Authorization, keep the default settings. The scope API.invoke is required — the JWT token issued using PIR credentials already contains this scope.


Other policies — traffic management, IP filter — are available from the policy palette. We will cover these in a later article in this series.

  

Step 7 — Configure the Backend Connection

Before deploying, configure authentication for the SuccessFactors target endpoint.

Click on the HTTP receiver adapter and:

  • Set Authentication to Basic
  • Enter the Credential Name — for example, sfsf (a credential stored in the Security Material section of Integration Suite, containing your SuccessFactors username and password)


Step 8 — Deploy

Save the artifact and click Deploy. Select Integration Cell as the Runtime Profile. The virtual host will be pre-populated.

 

Once deployed, the artifact status changes to Deployed.

 

Step 9 — Grab the MCP Endpoint URL

Navigate to Monitor → Integrations and APIs, set Runtime to Integration Cell, and click the Manage Integration Content tile → Started.

Your MCP Server artifact appears at the top. The endpoint URL is visible in the right panel — this is the URL you will configure in any AI agent.

 

Part 3: Connecting an AI Agent

The MCP endpoint can be connected to any MCP-compatible AI client — Joule (SAP's own AI assistant), Claude Desktop, Cline, GitHub Copilot, and others.

Getting Credentials

The agent authenticates using Process Integration Runtime (PIR) service key credentials. These are the same credentials used to invoke Integration Flows — retrieve them from the service key of your PIR instance on SAP BTP.

 

 

Connecting Joule

In this demo we use Joule Work Desktop — SAP's generative AI assistant and agent orchestrator. Joule supports external MCP server connections.

 


Once connected, Joule discovers all 12 tools exposed by the MCP server automatically. No further configuration is needed — the agent is ready to reason.

 

Connecting Claude / Cline

For Claude Desktop or Cline, the MCP configuration looks like this:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sfsf-company-car": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://<virtual-host>/sfsf",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Basic <base64-encoded-pir-credentials>"
      }
    }
  }
}


Part 4: The Experience — John Meets His AI Agent

ABC Corp has deployed the MCP server. John opens his AI assistant and types his questions exactly as he would ask a colleague.

Question 1 — "What are my car options?"

"I'm an employee looking to enroll in the company car benefit. What car models can I choose from, which vendors are recommended, and what lease service providers are available?"

The agent reasons silently and calls three tools in parallel: get_allowed_car_models, get_recommended_vendors, get_lease_providers.

Agent responds — 

Hi John! Here's what your company car benefit offers:

Approved Models: Toyota, Nissan, Volkswagen

Approved Vendors: Hertz, AVIS

Lease Financing:

Provider Monthly EMI Rate
AVIS Rental10.20%
LeasePlanContact HR for rate

Installments are paid monthly. Let me know if you'd like details on policy terms!

 

We can see the conversation with Joule and the tool calls it made on the right side.

 

Question 2 — "What is my enrollment and claim status?" 

"Can you show me the current company car benefit policies, my enrollment details, and whether I have any open claims?"

The agent calls get_car_benefit_policy, get_employee_car_enrollment, and get_employee_car_claims in parallel.

Agent responds:

Policy: Three active car benefit policies, all with monthly installment frequency.

Your Enrollment: You have an active enrollment (ID: 163585), but it is incomplete — your car model, vendor, and EMI amount have not been selected yet.

Claims: No claims on file.

Next step: Complete your enrollment by selecting a model and a financing option. Want help comparing them?

 

The Follow-up — Where the Agent Extends Beyond the Portal

"Which lease provider gives me the best deal if I go with a Toyota?"

This question sits outside what the portal was designed to show — it would normally mean a helpdesk ticket and a future sprint.

With the MCP agent, no new development is needed. The agent re-reads the lease provider and policy data already retrieved:

The only provider currently showing a configured EMI rate is AVIS Rental at 10.20% — LeasePlan's rate is not yet set in the system. For a Toyota, AVIS Rental is your best available option. I'd recommend confirming the exact monthly EMI with HR, since it depends on the car's purchase value.

Zero development. Zero tickets. Answered in seconds.

Part 5: Portal and Agent — Better Together

The portal and the MCP agent are not competing approaches — they serve different needs. The portal delivers a reliable, governed, designed experience for the majority of employee interactions. The agent handles the long tail: the follow-up question, the cross-entity comparison, the query no one thought to build a screen for.

Architecture Comparison

HR Portal:

John opens the portal
      │
      ▼
IT-built portal backend
      ├── API call 1 → AllowedModels
      ├── API call 2 → RecommendedVendors
      ├── API call 3 → LeaseServiceProvider
      ├── API call 4 → BenefitCompanyCar
      ├── API call 5 → CompanyCarEnrollment
      └── API call 6 → CompanyCarClaim
            │
            ▼
      JOIN logic in backend
            │
            ▼
      Designed screen renders the data
            │
            ▼
      John gets a reliable, consistent answer
      for questions the portal was built to answer

MCP Agent:

John's natural language question
      │
      ▼
AI Agent (Joule / Claude / Cline)
      │
      ▼
MCP Server on SAP Integration Suite
      ├── get_allowed_car_models    ──→ SF OData API 1
      ├── get_recommended_vendors   ──→ SF OData API 2
      ├── get_lease_providers       ──→ SF OData API 3
      ├── get_car_benefit_policy    ──→ SF OData API 4
      ├── get_employee_car_enrollment ─→ SF OData API 5
      └── get_employee_car_claims   ──→ SF OData API 6
            │
            ▼
      Agent synthesises, reasons, and responds
            │
            ▼
      John gets a conversational, contextual answer
      including questions no screen was built for

Key Takeaways

  1. The MCP server is configured, not coded. SAP Integration Suite's MCP wizard turns an OpenAPI spec into a deployable MCP endpoint — no custom server code required.

  2. Tool descriptions are the interface. The natural language description you write for each tool is what the agent reads when deciding what to call. It replaces the UI specification document.

  3. The same security infrastructure you already have applies. PIR credentials, OAuth, and Integration Cell's policy framework all work with the MCP endpoint out of the box.

  4. Any MCP-compatible agent connects. Joule, Claude, Cline, Copilot — once the MCP server is running, the choice of agent is independent of the integration work.


Thanks for reading. Hope you found it useful.

Have questions or want to share how your team is using MCP with SAP? Leave a comment below.

entry.title: Understanding the New API Rate Limit Headers in SAP SuccessFactors (with a Real Response Example)
entry.content:
Introduction

With the 2608 release (17 August 2026), SAP SuccessFactors began applying soft rate limits to all existing tenants, as part of the new SAP API Policy. Nothing is blocked yet, but every API response now carries standardized rate limit headers. SAP will later convert these soft limits to hard limits, and requests that exceed a hard limit will be rejected with HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests). SAP has not announced a date for that conversion, and new public APIs launched from 13 November 2026 will already be hard-limited.

API Rate Limit :

1. What is changing

Who Limit type When
All existing tenantsSoft (observed and flagged, not blocked)Since 2608 (17 Aug 2026)
New public APIsHard (HTTP 429)From 13 Nov 2026
Tenants provisioned on/after 1 Jan 2027HardFrom day one
Existing tenants, all APIsSoft converted to hardDate to be announced by SAP

Hard limits that were already set for specific tenants before this announcement stay in force. Limits apply at two scopes, and a request must satisfy both:

  • Resource level: per endpoint, and checked first.
  • Tenant level: shared by all integrations and users in the tenant, and checked second.

There are no per-user or per-integration limits, so one noisy integration can consume budget that other integrations need. Integration Center jobs and other internal SuccessFactors calls don't count, but SAP Integration Suite (BTP), middleware and custom apps do.

2. Reading the headers: a real example

I called the OData v2 entity BenefitEmployeeClaim with a plain GET request from Postman. The call returned 200 OK, and the response headers contained the following:

The two headers work as a pair. Ratelimit-Policy describes the rules, and Ratelimit shows where you currently stand.

 

Parameter Meaning
qQuota: the number of requests allowed in the window
wWindow length in seconds
mEnforcement mode (soft or hard)
rRequests remaining in the current window
tSeconds until the window resets

Interpreting this response:

  • customized-spike-arrest: 75 requests per 60 seconds, mode soft. There are 73 requests remaining and the counter resets in 26 seconds. In other words, 2 requests have been counted in this window.
  • tenant-quota: 600 requests per 60 seconds for the whole tenant. There are 598 remaining. (The enforcement mode is cut off in my screenshot, so check it in your own response.)

Two things are worth noting. First, the spike-arrest quota here (75/min) differs from the 25/min used in the example in SAP's KBA, so limits clearly vary by resource, and you shouldn't assume a single number. Second, in a hard-mode 429 response, the policy where r=0 is the one that was violated, and you can cross-reference it with Ratelimit-Policy to see its quota, window and mode.

3. What you should do now

  1. Start monitoring. Log the Ratelimit-Policy and Ratelimit headers in your middleware or API client. This is the best way to find out which integrations are close to their limits before enforcement begins.
  2. Add 429 handling now. On a 429, don't retry immediately. Honor the Retry-After header, use exponential backoff (for example 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) with random jitter, and log every 429 as an integration health signal.
  3. Reduce unnecessary calls. Batch requests where possible, cache reference data such as picklists, pull only records changed since the last run, and stagger scheduled jobs instead of starting them all on the hour.
  4. Leave headroom. Design for roughly 70–80% of the limit under normal load, so retries and peaks don't push you over.
  5. Plan for go-lives. SAP has confirmed an exemption process with an expiry date for go-live, hypercare and peak periods. You request it by logging a case under component LOD-SF-INT-API.

 

 

Soft limits give you a grace period. Every SuccessFactors API response already tells you which policies apply to it, how much budget is left and when it resets. Use that period to find your heaviest integrations, add proper 429 handling and bring call volumes down. When SAP announces the move to hard limits, integrations that already monitor the headers and back off correctly shouldn't notice a difference.

For the complete list of endpoint-specific limits (92+ endpoints), see the Rate Limits page in the SAP SuccessFactors API Reference Guide (OData V2) on SAP Help Portal.

References

  • SAP Note 3792944, FAQ: API Rate Limits for SAP SuccessFactors
  • SAP Help Portal, SAP SuccessFactors API Reference Guide (OData V2), Rate Limits
